terms.name: Graph
terms.description: graph concept consisting of nodes connected by edges.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Graph is a mathematical structure consisting of nodes (vertices) connected by edges (links or relationships). This abstract model provides a natural and powerful way to represent networks of interconnected information, from social networks and citation graphs to knowledge graphs and biological pathways. Graph theory provides formal foundations for analyzing connectivity, paths, and structural properties.

Nodes and edges: Nodes represent entities—people, places, concepts, documents, or any objects of interest. Edges represent relationships—friendship between people, citations between papers, part-whole connections between concepts. Together, nodes and edges form networks that can be analyzed, visualized, and queried using graph algorithms and data structures.

Directed vs. undirected: In directed graphs, edges have direction—'A follows B' doesn't imply 'B follows A.' In undirected graphs, edges are bidirectional—'A is married to B' means 'B is married to A.' RDF graphs are directed—each triple has a specific subject and object. Property graphs can have directed or undirected edges depending on relationship semantics.

Labeled and attributed graphs: Simple graphs have just nodes and edges. Labeled graphs add types to edges—'knows,' 'works for,' 'contains.' Property graphs add arbitrary attributes to both nodes and edges. RDF represents labeled graphs where edge labels are predicates. These extensions make graphs richer and more expressive for modeling real-world information.

Graph algorithms: Graph theory provides algorithms for analyzing structure: shortest path finding (how is A connected to B?), centrality analysis (which nodes are most important?), community detection (what clusters exist?), and reachability (can you get from A to B?). These algorithms enable insights from network structure that aren't apparent from individual relationships.

Why graphs for data: Many real-world systems are inherently networked—social connections, organizational structures, supply chains, neural pathways, transportation systems. Graphs naturally model these interconnections. Graph queries traverse relationships efficiently, making them ideal for questions like 'friends of friends' or 'all dependencies' that are complex in relational databases.

Graph databases: Graph databases store data as graphs and optimize for graph traversal and pattern matching. They include RDF triplestores (like GraphDB, Stardog) and property graph databases (like Neo4j, Amazon Neptune). The choice between models depends on whether you prioritize standards-based semantic interoperability (RDF) or flexible schema and query performance (property graphs).

Related: RDF Graph is the semantic web instantiation. Property Graph is an alternative model. Triple forms RDF graphs. Graph Fundamentals is the category.

terms.name: TriG
terms.description: serialization format that extends Turtle to support named graphs by grouping triples into graph blocks.
terms.additionalInformation:
TriG (Turtle + Named Graphs) extends Turtle syntax to support named graphs by introducing graph blocks that group triples. It enables representing complete RDF datasets—collections of multiple named graphs plus an optional default graph—in a single readable file, combining Turtle's human-friendly syntax with dataset-level expressiveness.

Named graph syntax: TriG extends Turtle by wrapping triple groups in graph blocks: <http://example.org/graph1> { :alice :name "Alice" . :bob :name "Bob" . } declares that these triples belong to the named graph identified by that URI. Multiple graph blocks in one file represent multiple graphs, enabling dataset-level authoring.

Default graph: TriG allows triples outside graph blocks, which belong to the default (unnamed) graph. This mirrors dataset semantics where you have multiple named graphs plus one default graph. The default graph often contains metadata about the named graphs themselves.

Example: A TriG file might be: @prefix : <http://example.org/> . :metadata { :graph1 :created "2023-06-15" . } :graph1 { :alice :name "Alice" ; :age 42 . } :graph2 { :bob :name "Bob" ; :age 38 . } This represents a dataset with metadata in the default graph and data in two named graphs.

Use cases: TriG excels when you need to partition data into logical graphs—separating data by source, time period, provenance, or trust level. It's ideal for representing data provenance (which graph came from which source), versioning (different graphs for different versions), and multi-tenant scenarios (one graph per customer).

Processing datasets: RDF datasets are the natural model for scenarios where graph identity matters—tracking which source asserted which facts, temporal datasets where each time slice is a graph, or federated data where each contributor's data stays separate. TriG provides a readable serialization for these scenarios.

Related: Turtle is the base syntax. N-Quads provides similar capabilities in line-based format. Named Graph is what TriG represents. Serialization Formats includes TriG. Dataset is the model TriG encodes.

terms.name: Knowledge Graph
terms.description: paradigm of a network of interconnected entities and their relationships, often combining data from multiple sources.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Knowledge Graph is a network of interconnected entities and their relationships, typically combining data from multiple sources with explicit semantics that machines can process. Popularized by Google in 2012 to enhance search results, knowledge graphs have become a mainstream approach for organizing enterprise information, powering AI applications, and integrating heterogeneous data.

Beyond simple graphs: What distinguishes a knowledge graph from a generic graph database is the emphasis on semantics, real-world entities, and integration across diverse sources. A knowledge graph doesn't just store connections—it represents what things are, how they relate, and what those relationships mean. This enables reasoning, question answering, and sophisticated analytics beyond simple graph traversal.

Entity-centric perspective: Knowledge graphs organize information around entities (people, places, organizations, products, concepts) rather than documents or records. All facts about an entity come together regardless of source system. This entity-centric view supports applications like customer 360 views, master data management, research graphs connecting publications and researchers, and product knowledge that combines specifications, reviews, and competitive intelligence.

Schema flexibility: Unlike relational databases requiring predefined schemas, knowledge graphs embrace schema flexibility. New properties can be added to entities without altering table structures. Entities can have different property sets. This flexibility facilitates incremental development and integration of new data sources, though it requires discipline to maintain quality without rigid schemas.

Real-world applications: Google uses its Knowledge Graph to enhance search with information panels about entities. Amazon's product graph connects products, categories, reviews, and customer behavior. LinkedIn's Economic Graph models professionals, companies, skills, and jobs. Enterprise knowledge graphs integrate HR, finance, operations, and customer data for analytics and AI. Use cases span search, recommendation, fraud detection, drug discovery, and regulatory compliance.

Building knowledge graphs: Construction typically involves entity extraction from text, database extraction and transformation, linking entities across sources through entity resolution, and enrichment from external datasets. Ontologies or schemas provide structure. Validation ensures quality. The process is often iterative—starting with core entities and relationships, then expanding coverage and adding sophistication.

Knowledge graph vs. ontology: Ontologies emphasize formal definitions, logical rigor, and reasoning. Knowledge graphs emphasize practical integration, broad coverage, and application value. Many knowledge graphs use lightweight schemas or no formal ontology at all, relying on common vocabularies and linking rather than logical axioms. Others combine both—ontologies for the model layer, massive instance data in the graph.

Related: Semantic Web provides foundational technologies. Linked Data emphasizes web-scale linking. RDF Graph is a common implementation. Ontology may provide structure. Reasoning enables inference.

terms.name: Inverse Functional Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if two individuals share the same value, they must be the same individual.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Inverse Functional Property is one where if two different subjects have the same value, they must actually be the same individual. This characteristic provides powerful entity resolution—if a property uniquely identifies individuals, finding two entities with the same value for that property means they're actually the same entity, not duplicates.

Reverse uniqueness: Where functional properties say each subject has at most one value, inverse functional says each value has at most one subject. If property P is inverse functional, 'A P X' and 'B P X' implies A and B are the same. The shared value X identifies a unique individual, so different names must refer to the same entity.

Identity and deduplication: Inverse functional properties enable automatic entity resolution. If email addresses are inverse functional and two person records share an email, they represent the same person. A reasoner can infer they're identical using owl:sameAs. This supports data integration and deduplication without custom matching algorithms.

Common examples: Unique identifiers are inverse functional—social security numbers, employee IDs, ISBNs, DOIs. If properly unique, email addresses might be inverse functional. License plate numbers, passport numbers, and other government IDs are typically inverse functional within their scope.

Scope and validity: Inverse functionality depends on scope. An employee ID is inverse functional within one company but not globally—different companies reuse IDs. Email addresses are inverse functional if each belongs to one person, but shared accounts violate this. Declaring properties inverse functional requires ensuring the uniqueness assumption holds in your data.

Reasoning implications: Inverse functional properties create owl:sameAs inferences prolifically in large datasets. If you have millions of records and an inverse functional property, finding shared values generates potentially millions of sameAs statements. This can explode the reasoning space and severely impact performance.

Practical considerations: Use inverse functional properties carefully. They're powerful for small-to-medium datasets with good data quality. For large datasets with potentially dirty data (duplicate IDs, shared emails), the inferences may be incorrect or overwhelming. Sometimes modeling identifiers explicitly rather than using inverse functionality gives better control.

Related: Functional Property is related but opposite direction. Property Characteristic is the category. sameAs is inferred. Reasoning uses this for entity resolution.

terms.name: CURIE
terms.description: naming concept for a compact URI that uses a prefix and local name separated by a colon.
terms.additionalInformation:
A CURIE (Compact URI) is a shortened URI notation using a prefix and local name separated by a colon, providing human-readable alternatives to full IRIs. CURIEs make RDF data more readable and writable by replacing verbose full URIs with concise prefixed forms like foaf:Person instead of <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Person>.

Prefix mechanism: CURIEs work by defining prefix bindings that map short names to namespace IRIs. Define foaf: as shorthand for http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/, then foaf:Person expands to the full IRI. Prefixes are local to a document or context, not globally standardized.

Readability improvement: Full IRIs are verbose and hard to read: <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Person> <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#subClassOf> <http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/Agent>. With CURIEs: foaf:Person rdfs:subClassOf foaf:Agent. The meaning is clearer and the data is scannable.

Turtle and SPARQL: RDF serialization formats like Turtle and query languages like SPARQL use CURIE syntax extensively. Prefix declarations at the document start define mappings, then CURIEs appear throughout. This combination of compact notation with full IRI precision balances human and machine needs.

Context dependency: CURIEs are context-dependent—the same CURIE might expand differently in different documents with different prefix bindings. ex:Person means different IRIs depending on what namespace ex: is bound to. This context dependency requires careful prefix management.

Safe CURIEs: Some specifications use safe CURIE notation [foaf:Person] with brackets to distinguish CURIEs from literal text that might contain colons. This prevents ambiguity in contexts where both CURIEs and plain text appear.

Related: IRI and URI are what CURIEs abbreviate. Namespace and Prefix define the expansion mapping. Turtle and SPARQL use CURIE syntax. Identifiers & Namespaces is the category.

terms.name: Subject
terms.description: triple component that identifies the resource being described, typically a URI or blank node.
terms.additionalInformation:
The Subject is the first element of an RDF triple, identifying the resource that the statement is about. It represents the entity being described—the 'who' or 'what' that has properties or relationships. In graph terms, the subject is the source node from which an edge (the predicate) points to a target (the object).

URI or blank node: Subjects are typically URIs that globally identify resources—<http://example.org/person/alice> identifies a specific person. Alternatively, subjects can be blank nodes representing anonymous resources relevant only in local context. Literals cannot be subjects in standard RDF (though RDF-star relaxes this for quoted triples).

What can be a subject: Anything you can identify with a URI can be a subject—people, places, organizations, documents, concepts, events, physical objects, or abstract ideas. The subject represents the entity you're making assertions about. Multiple triples can share the same subject, each describing a different property or relationship of that entity.

Grouping by subject: RDF serialization formats like Turtle group triples by subject for readability. All statements about a person appear together, with the subject written once and properties listed beneath. This reflects how we naturally think—describing an entity with all its attributes rather than scattering facts across the dataset.

Subject in queries: SPARQL queries often start by constraining subjects—'find triples where the subject is this specific resource' or 'where the subject has type Person.' The S-P-O indexing in triplestores optimizes for subject-based access, making it efficient to retrieve all properties of a given resource.

Subject-centric vs. object-centric: RDF is subject-oriented—statements flow from subject to object. To express reciprocal relationships, you need inverse properties or separate triples. If :alice :knows :bob, that doesn't automatically mean :bob :knows :alice unless you explicitly state it or define :knows as symmetric.

Related: Predicate and Object are the other triple components. Triple combines all three. URI and Blank Node identify subjects. RDF Graph is composed of triples.

terms.name: broader
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is more general than another within the same concept scheme.
terms.additionalInformation:
The skos:broader property indicates that one concept is more general than another within the same SKOS concept scheme, creating hierarchical relationships. Broader/narrower relationships build the taxonomic backbone of thesauri and taxonomies, organizing concepts from specific to general.

Hierarchical organization: Broader creates parent-child relationships: 'Dog' broader 'Mammal', 'Sedan' broader 'Car', 'Python' broader 'Programming Language'. Each broader link moves up the abstraction hierarchy toward more general categories. Chains of broader links create complete taxonomies.

Transitive reasoning: Broader is transitive—if A broader B and B broader C, then A broader C. This enables reasoning about full hierarchical paths. Queries for general concepts can include all narrower descendants automatically through transitive closure.

Inverse of narrower: If A broader B, then B narrower A. These are inverse relationships representing the same hierarchy from opposite directions. SKOS requires only one direction to be asserted—the other can be inferred.

Search and navigation: Broader links support hierarchical navigation in user interfaces—from specific topics to containing categories. They enable query expansion—searching for 'Vehicles' can include results tagged with narrower concepts like 'Cars,' 'Trucks,' 'Bicycles.'

Related: narrower is the inverse. broadMatch applies across schemes. Taxonomy uses broader relationships. SKOS defines broader.

terms.name: Graph Concept
terms.description: semantic modeling building block representing the core concepts of graph-based data models.

terms.name: Symmetric Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if A relates to B, then B relates to A
terms.additionalInformation:
A Symmetric Property is one where if A relates to B, then B relates to A. This characteristic captures bidirectional relationships that work the same in both directions. Common symmetric properties include knows, sibling, connectedTo, and adjacentTo—relationships where if one entity has the relationship to another, the reverse automatically holds.

Bidirectional inference: Symmetry eliminates redundancy. State 'Alice knows Bob' once, and a reasoner infers 'Bob knows Alice' automatically. You don't need to store both directions explicitly, halving storage requirements for symmetric relationships while ensuring bidirectional queries work correctly.

Classic examples: Social relationships like 'friend,' 'colleague,' or 'spouse' are typically symmetric (in idealized models—reality can be more complex). Physical relationships like 'adjacent to,' 'connected to,' or 'shares border with' are symmetric. Equivalence relationships like 'sameAs' or 'exactMatch' must be symmetric.

Not all relationships are symmetric: Many properties have clear direction. 'Parent of' isn't symmetric—your parent isn't your child. 'Knows' might seem symmetric but could model directed awareness. 'Employs' and 'works for' are inverses but neither is symmetric. Incorrectly declaring properties as symmetric creates wrong inferences.

Symmetry with other characteristics: Properties can be both symmetric and transitive. 'Connected to' in a network might have both—if A connects to B, then B connects to A (symmetry), and if A connects to B and B connects to C, then A connects to C (transitivity). This combination enables powerful network reasoning.

Implementation considerations: Symmetric properties can be stored in either direction—the reasoner generates the inverse as needed. Some systems normalize by storing relationships in canonical direction (lower URI to higher URI), reducing duplication. Query optimization must handle symmetry to ensure finding relationships regardless of assertion direction.

Related: Property Characteristic is the category. Asymmetric Property is the opposite. Inverse Property models bidirectionality differently. sameAs is inherently symmetric.

terms.name: IRI
terms.description: semantic resource identifier that extends URIs to support characters from all languages and scripts.
terms.additionalInformation:
An IRI (Internationalized Resource Identifier) extends URIs to support characters from all languages and scripts, not just ASCII. IRIs enable identifiers containing Chinese, Arabic, Cyrillic, emoji, or any Unicode characters, making the semantic web truly international and accessible to users of all languages.

Unicode support: While URIs are limited to ASCII characters (with percent-encoding for others), IRIs natively support full Unicode. Identifiers can include native language characters: http://例え.jp/人物/太郎 (Japanese), http://example.org/شخص/محمد (Arabic). This linguistic inclusivity matters for global adoption and usability.

RDF standard identifiers: Modern RDF standards use IRIs as the default identifier format. All RDF specifications since RDF 1.1 use IRI terminology. Tools and libraries must support IRIs, handling Unicode properly in parsing, serialization, and comparison.

Normalization: IRIs require Unicode normalization—different byte sequences can represent visually identical characters. NFD vs. NFC normalization, combining characters, and equivalences must be handled correctly. Tools must normalize consistently to ensure IRI comparison works correctly.

Backward compatibility: IRIs are a superset of URIs—every URI is a valid IRI. Systems supporting IRIs can also handle URIs. This backward compatibility eases migration from URI-only systems to IRI-supporting infrastructure.

Conversion to URIs: When interfacing with systems requiring ASCII URIs, IRIs can be converted using percent-encoding. The IRI is transformed to a URI by encoding non-ASCII characters. This enables interoperability with legacy systems while maintaining IRI benefits in modern components.

Related: URI is the ASCII predecessor. CURIE provides compact notation. Identifiers & Namespaces is the category. Namespace and Prefix use IRIs.

terms.name: Datatype
terms.description: value specification of how literal values should be interpreted and compared
terms.additionalInformation:
A Datatype specifies how literal values should be interpreted and compared, such as integers, decimals, dates, booleans, or strings. Datatypes ensure consistent handling of typed data across systems—numbers sort numerically, dates enable temporal reasoning, booleans support logical operations. RDF uses XML Schema datatypes as the standard type system.

Type system: RDF adopts XML Schema datatypes (XSD): xsd:string for text, xsd:integer and xsd:decimal for numbers, xsd:date and xsd:dateTime for temporal values, xsd:boolean for true/false, and many others covering durations, byte sequences, and specialized types. This standard type system enables interoperability.

Value space and lexical space: Datatypes define both what values are valid (value space) and how those values are written (lexical space). For xsd:integer, the value 42 can be written '42', '+42', or '042'—different lexical forms represent the same value. Datatypes specify equivalence rules.

Comparison and operations: Datatypes determine how values compare and what operations apply. Numeric types support arithmetic and numeric comparison. Date types enable temporal reasoning. String types support pattern matching and concatenation. Proper datatypes enable meaningful processing beyond treating everything as text.

Custom datatypes: Beyond XSD built-ins, applications can define custom datatypes for domain-specific values. However, custom types reduce interoperability—other systems may not understand specialized datatypes or know how to validate or process them.

Related: Literal has datatypes. Datatype Property has datatype ranges. Values includes typed literals. Range may specify datatypes.

terms.name: Unnamed Individual
terms.description: individual represented by a blank node without a global URI identifier.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Unnamed Individual (also called anonymous individual) is represented by a blank node that has no global URI identifier. Used for supporting or intermediate entities that don't need to be referenced outside their local context, unnamed individuals enable modeling complex structures without proliferating global identifiers for every piece of information.

Blank nodes for anonymity: Blank nodes provide local identity within a graph but no global identity across graphs. They're useful for entities that exist only to support other descriptions—a mailing address that's part of a person record, a measurement value with units and precision, or a temporal qualification of a fact. These supporting objects don't need their own URIs.

When to use unnamed individuals: Use blank nodes for entities that are components of larger structures without independent significance. An address described inline as part of a person's data doesn't need a URI—it matters only in context of that person. Contrast with a place that multiple people reference; that should be a named individual so references can be shared.

Querying limitations: Blank nodes are harder to query and reference than named individuals. You can't directly query for 'all triples about blank node X' because X has no stable global identifier. Blank nodes are matched by their property patterns. Overusing blank nodes can make data less discoverable and harder to integrate.

Merging challenges: When merging RDF graphs, blank nodes from different sources are assumed to be different entities even if they have identical properties. If two datasets each describe Alice's address using blank nodes, merging doesn't recognize them as the same address—you get two distinct anonymous addresses. Named individuals with shared URIs merge automatically.

Skolemization: Some systems convert blank nodes to named individuals through skolemization—assigning them URIs systematically. This trades the simplicity of blank nodes for the referenceability of URIs. Skolemized URIs are often in a special namespace indicating they were generated rather than semantically meaningful.

Related: Named Individual has explicit identity. Blank Node is the technical implementation. Individual is the general concept. Identifiers & Namespaces covers identification approaches.

terms.name: Application Ontology
terms.description: ontology tailored to the specific needs and processes of a particular application or use case.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Application Ontology is tailored to the specific requirements of a particular application, use case, or project. It typically combines and extends elements from upper ontologies and domain ontologies, adding application-specific concepts, workflows, and constraints. While less reusable than domain ontologies, application ontologies directly serve operational needs.

Specificity for purpose: Where domain ontologies aim for broad coverage of a field, application ontologies optimize for specific tasks. An application for clinical trial recruitment might combine patient ontologies with trial protocol concepts and add workflow states specific to the recruitment process. This specificity enables precisely modeling the application's logic and data.

Integration of multiple domains: Applications often span multiple domains, requiring concepts from each. A supply chain application might combine manufacturing ontologies (for products), logistics ontologies (for transportation), and financial ontologies (for costs and payments). The application ontology integrates these domains with application-specific glue concepts and relationships.

Implementation coupling: Application ontologies often reflect implementation details—specific business rules, workflow states, or system interfaces. A fraud detection application might model concepts like 'suspicious transaction flag' or 'investigation case status' that make sense only within that application. This tight coupling to implementation makes application ontologies less reusable but more immediately useful.

Evolution pace: Application ontologies evolve as application requirements change. New features require new concepts. Changing business rules modify constraints. This rapid evolution contrasts with domain ontologies that change more slowly to maintain stability for their many users. Application ontologies can be more agile because they serve fewer stakeholders.

Development approach: Application ontologies are often developed iteratively alongside application code. Initial versions capture core concepts, later versions add sophistication as understanding deepens. This agile approach contrasts with domain ontologies that typically require extensive upfront design to serve diverse future needs.

Reuse strategy: Smart application ontology development maximizes reuse of standard vocabularies and domain ontologies for broadly applicable concepts, creating custom terms only for application-specific needs. This balances interoperability (reused terms can be understood by other systems) with precision (custom terms exactly fit the application).

Related: Domain Ontology provides broader foundation. Application Profile similarly tailors general standards. Ontology general concept. Knowledge Representation broader context.

terms.name: Linking Mechanism
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing the technique and property for connecting related concepts across different vocabularies, ontologies, or datasets to enable data integration.

terms.name: OWL
terms.description: standard semantic markup language for creating complex ontologies with logical axioms and constraints.
terms.additionalInformation:
OWL (Web Ontology Language) is a rich semantic markup language for creating sophisticated ontologies with logical axioms, complex restrictions, and reasoning capabilities. Based on description logics, OWL enables expressing complex domain knowledge formally, supporting automated classification, consistency checking, and inference of implicit knowledge.

Description logic foundation: OWL is grounded in description logics, formal logic systems with well-understood computational properties. This foundation enables provably correct reasoning and provides theoretical guarantees about what can be inferred and how expensive it will be computationally.

Expressive constructs: OWL extends RDFS with property characteristics (transitive, symmetric, functional), class expressions (union, intersection, complement), cardinality restrictions, property chains, disjointness, and equivalence. These constructs enable precise definitions capturing complex domain requirements.

OWL profiles: OWL 2 defines profiles—subsets optimized for different uses. OWL 2 EL enables efficient reasoning over large ontologies with simpler expressions. OWL 2 QL optimizes for query answering over databases. OWL 2 RL enables rule-based implementation. Profiles balance expressiveness with computational tractability.

Reasoning capabilities: OWL reasoners can classify individuals based on property values, organize classes into inferred hierarchies, detect inconsistencies, and derive new facts from axioms. This automated reasoning distinguishes OWL from simpler schema languages.

When to use OWL: Choose OWL when you need sophisticated reasoning, precise logical definitions, or formal rigor. Scientific domains, regulatory compliance, and complex integration scenarios benefit from OWL's power. Simple use cases may find it overcomplicated.

Related: RDFS is simpler alternative. Ontology is built with OWL. Reasoning uses OWL axioms. Class, Property, Restriction are OWL constructs. Standards includes OWL.

terms.name: SPARQL Endpoint
terms.description: data service that accepts SPARQL queries over HTTP and returns results.
terms.additionalInformation:
A SPARQL Endpoint is a web service that accepts SPARQL queries over HTTP and returns results in various formats. It provides programmatic access to RDF datasets, enabling applications to query semantic data remotely without requiring direct database access or data download. SPARQL endpoints are the standard interface for RDF data access.

HTTP-based querying: SPARQL endpoints use HTTP GET or POST to accept queries and return results. Query strings are URL-encoded or sent in request bodies. Results come in multiple formats: SPARQL results XML/JSON for SELECT queries, RDF formats for CONSTRUCT/DESCRIBE. This HTTP-based protocol enables language-agnostic access.

Public endpoints: Major knowledge bases expose public SPARQL endpoints: DBpedia, Wikidata, biological databases, library catalogs, government data. These endpoints democratize access to vast amounts of structured knowledge, enabling applications to leverage public data without local copies.

Enterprise endpoints: Organizations deploy internal SPARQL endpoints for accessing corporate knowledge graphs, master data, or integrated views across business systems. Authentication, authorization, and rate limiting control access. Endpoints become the standard query interface for semantic enterprise data.

Federated queries: SPARQL federation allows one query to access multiple endpoints, combining results automatically. This enables queries spanning organizational boundaries—integrating internal data with external knowledge without copying or synchronization.

Related: SPARQL is the query language. Triplestore implements endpoints. RDF Graph is queried. Access & Publication includes endpoints.

terms.name: closeMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts are sufficiently similar to be used interchangeably in some applications.
terms.additionalInformation:
The skos:closeMatch property indicates that two concepts from different SKOS concept schemes are sufficiently similar that they can be used interchangeably in some applications, though they're not exactly equivalent. CloseMatch represents near-synonymy or significant semantic overlap while acknowledging differences that matter in some contexts.

Near equivalence: CloseMatch applies when concepts are very similar but have subtle differences in scope, emphasis, or definition. Your 'Data Analysis' category might be a close match to a standard 'Data Analytics' category—similar enough for most purposes but not identical. Applications can treat them as equivalent when precision doesn't matter.

Weaker than exactMatch: The distinction between exact and close matching reflects real-world ambiguity in concept alignment. Exact means you're confident the concepts are interchangeable. Close means they're similar enough to be useful for discovery or approximation but might have differences that matter in precise contexts.

Symmetric but use carefully with transitivity: CloseMatch is symmetric (if A closeMatch B, then B closeMatch A) but transitivity is questionable. If A is close to B and B is close to C, A might not be close to C—semantic drift accumulates through chains. Most systems don't treat closeMatch as transitive to avoid creating spurious equivalences.

Use cases: CloseMatch supports exploratory search, recommendation systems, and approximate categorization. When finding documents about 'machine learning,' including those tagged with close matches like 'artificial intelligence' or 'statistical learning' improves recall. Users can then filter based on precise distinctions if needed.

Related: exactMatch for stricter equivalence. relatedMatch for general association. broadMatch and narrowMatch for hierarchical relationships. Linking & Alignment includes closeMatch.

terms.name: Controlled Vocabulary
terms.description: knowledge organization system that provides an organized list of terms with defined meanings used consistently to tag or describe content.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Controlled Vocabulary is an organized list of terms with defined meanings, used consistently to tag, categorize, or describe content. It's the simplest form of knowledge organization—establishing agreed-upon terminology to prevent ambiguity, synonyms, and inconsistent usage. Controlled vocabularies ensure that everyone uses the same term for the same concept, enabling reliable search and consistent categorization.

Vocabulary control: Without control, different people use different words for the same thing—one person says 'client,' another 'customer,' a third 'buyer.' Searches miss results, analytics count the same thing multiple times, and integration fails. Controlled vocabularies solve this by designating one preferred term and documenting that everyone should use it. Documentation may note non-preferred synonyms but directs usage to the preferred form.

Scope notes: Good controlled vocabularies include scope notes that define exactly what each term means and when to use it. 'Client' might be defined as 'individual or organization receiving professional services,' distinguishing it from 'customer' (anyone making a purchase). These definitions prevent ambiguity and guide consistent application.

Simple lists to complex schemes: The simplest controlled vocabulary is just a list of approved terms—valid product categories, department names, status values. More sophisticated versions add hierarchical organization (creating taxonomies) or semantic relationships (creating thesauri). The level of structure should match the use case complexity.

Common applications: Organizations use controlled vocabularies for tagging documents with keywords, selecting values in data entry forms, categorizing support tickets, assigning topic codes to content, and many other classification tasks. The vocabulary ensures that everyone picks from the same options, enabling meaningful aggregation and filtering.

Maintenance and evolution: Controlled vocabularies require governance—who can add new terms? How are definitions changed? When are terms deprecated? Without governance, vocabularies grow uncontrolled, accumulate duplicates, and lose consistency. Even simple vocabularies benefit from designated owners and change processes.

Multilingual vocabularies: International organizations maintain vocabularies in multiple languages with equivalent terms defined across languages. Each concept has labels in English, French, Spanish, etc. This enables consistent categorization across language boundaries while supporting users in their native languages.

Related: Taxonomy adds hierarchical structure. Thesaurus adds richer relationships. Authority File is similar. SKOS provides RDF representation. Knowledge Organization Systems is the broader category.

terms.name: Domain Ontology
terms.description: ontology that models concepts and relationships specific to a particular field or area of knowledge.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Domain Ontology models concepts, relationships, and rules specific to a particular field of knowledge or area of practice, such as healthcare, finance, manufacturing, or legal services. Domain ontologies capture specialized knowledge that experts understand but that needs formal representation for computational use, data integration, and knowledge sharing.

Specialized knowledge: Each domain has concepts and relationships that make sense only within that context. Healthcare has diagnoses, treatments, and clinical pathways. Finance has securities, trades, and portfolio allocations. Manufacturing has assemblies, bill of materials, and production schedules. Domain ontologies formalize this specialized vocabulary with precise definitions and constraints.

Expert-driven development: Creating domain ontologies requires both ontology engineering skills and deep domain expertise. Ideally, domain experts collaborate with knowledge engineers to identify concepts, define relationships, and specify rules. This collaboration ensures the ontology captures actual domain practice rather than theoretical abstractions that don't match reality.

Examples: The Gene Ontology describes biological processes, molecular functions, and cellular components. The Financial Industry Business Ontology (FIBO) models financial instruments, organizations, and contracts. SNOMED CT provides comprehensive clinical terminology. These ontologies often involve thousands of classes and properties, representing decades of expert curation.

Integration foundation: Domain ontologies enable integrating data from different systems within a field. Multiple electronic health record systems can map to SNOMED CT, enabling patient data exchange. Different trading systems can align to FIBO, enabling regulatory reporting. The shared ontology provides a common language that bridges system-specific schemas.

Reuse of upper ontologies: Many domain ontologies extend upper ontologies, inheriting fundamental concepts and adding domain-specific detail. A biomedical ontology might use BFO's distinctions between continuants and occurrents, then define specific proteins, diseases, and biological processes. This grounds domain concepts in broader formal frameworks while maintaining domain specificity.

Maintenance communities: Successful domain ontologies often have governance structures, curation teams, and regular release cycles. The Gene Ontology has hundreds of curators worldwide. SNOMED CT is maintained by an international organization. These communities manage evolution, quality control, and alignment with standards—treating ontologies as critical shared infrastructure.

Related: Upper Ontology may provide foundation. Application Ontology specializes domains further. Ontology general concept. Vocabulary and Controlled Vocabulary are lighter-weight alternatives.

terms.name: Data Asset
terms.description: semantic modeling component representing an organized collection of data that is published, shared, or managed as a discrete unit.

terms.name: related
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts are associated in meaning within the same concept scheme.
terms.additionalInformation:
The skos:related property indicates that two concepts within the same SKOS scheme are semantically associated, without being hierarchically related or equivalent. Related relationships capture the associative dimension of thesauri, connecting concepts that commonly occur together or influence each other.

Associative relationships: Related connects concepts that aren't hierarchically organized but have meaningful connections. 'Climate Change' might be related to 'Renewable Energy,' 'Software Development' to 'Project Management,' 'Diabetes' to 'Diet.' These aren't broader/narrower relationships—they're peer associations.

Symmetric relationship: Related is symmetric—if A related to B, then B related to A. The association works in both directions, enabling bidirectional discovery. This differs from broader/narrower which are asymmetric.

See-also and discovery: Related supports 'see also' functionality in information retrieval. When viewing documents about one concept, showing related concepts helps users discover associated topics they might not have considered. This improves exploratory search and serendipitous discovery.

Related: broader and narrower for hierarchical relationships. relatedMatch applies across schemes. Thesaurus uses related extensively. SKOS defines related.

terms.name: SKOS
terms.description: standard for representing taxonomies, thesauri, and classification schemes in RDF.
terms.additionalInformation:
SKOS (Simple Knowledge Organization System) is an RDF vocabulary for representing taxonomies, thesauri, classification schemes, and controlled vocabularies. SKOS enables publishing traditional knowledge organization systems as linked data, making library classifications, subject headings, and institutional taxonomies available for reuse and integration across the web.

Bridging worlds: SKOS connects traditional library science knowledge organization with semantic web technologies. Decades-old classification schemes and thesauri can be expressed in RDF, gaining web identifiers, machine-readability, and linkability while preserving their structure and semantics.

Core concepts: SKOS models knowledge organization through concepts (ideas or meanings), concept schemes (collections of concepts), and relationships (broader, narrower, related for hierarchy and association; exactMatch, closeMatch for alignment). Labels (preferred, alternative, hidden) support multilingual terminology and synonym management.

Lightweight approach: SKOS intentionally provides simpler semantics than OWL. It focuses on practical knowledge organization rather than logical rigor. This simplicity makes it accessible to information professionals without logic or ontology expertise and keeps implementations straightforward.

Real-world adoption: Major libraries, archives, museums, and government agencies publish their classification schemes and subject headings as SKOS. Library of Congress Subject Headings, Getty Art & Architecture Thesaurus, and national library authorities are available as SKOS vocabularies.

Related: Taxonomy, Thesaurus, Classification Scheme are represented in SKOS. Concept Scheme is the SKOS container. broader, narrower, related are SKOS relationships. Standards includes SKOS.

terms.name: Open World Assumption
terms.description: reasoning concept where the absence of a statement does not mean it is false, only that it is unknown.
terms.additionalInformation:
The Open World Assumption (OWA) is a fundamental principle in semantic web reasoning that treats the absence of information as unknown rather than false. If a statement isn't explicitly present in the knowledge base, it might be true, false, or simply not yet known—you can't conclude anything from its absence alone.

Contrast with databases: This is radically different from traditional SQL databases, which operate under the Closed World Assumption. In SQL, if you query for someone's email address and get no result, the system treats that as 'this person has no email.' Under OWA, the same absence means only 'we don't know if this person has an email.' This distinction fundamentally changes how queries, constraints, and validation work.

Example: Suppose your knowledge base contains Alice worksFor CompanyX but says nothing about Bob. Under OWA, you cannot conclude that Bob doesn't work for CompanyX—maybe that fact just hasn't been added yet, or comes from a different data source you haven't integrated. A query for 'all people who don't work for CompanyX' cannot return Bob unless there's an explicit statement that he works elsewhere or that he's unemployed.

Why it matters: OWA enables incremental knowledge building and data integration from multiple sources. You can merge datasets without conflicts arising from missing information. It's essential for the web-scale linked data vision where no single source has complete information. However, it makes certain types of queries and constraints more complex to express.

Practical implications: Validation often requires explicitly stating negative constraints rather than assuming absence means violation. When you want to enforce 'every person must have exactly one birthdate,' you need to use cardinality constraints or SHACL shapes—you can't just check if the birthdate is missing. Query patterns that work in SQL (like 'find people without email addresses') require different approaches in SPARQL.

When OWA causes confusion: Data architects coming from SQL backgrounds often find OWA counterintuitive initially. A common mistake is expecting that lack of a triple means 'no' when it really means 'unknown.' Tools like SHACL help by providing closed-world validation on top of open-world data, giving you the best of both approaches for different use cases.

Related: Closed World Assumption is the opposite approach used in databases. Reasoning operates under OWA. SHACL provides closed-world validation. Validation strategies differ significantly under OWA.

terms.name: Validation Mechanism
terms.description: semantic modeling process of checking whether data conforms to specified constraints, shapes, or rules.

terms.name: Shape
terms.description: validation mechanism that defines a set of constraints for what valid data should look like for a particular use case.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Shape in SHACL defines a set of constraints that describe what valid RDF data should look like for a particular use case. Shapes specify required properties, allowed datatypes, cardinality restrictions, value patterns, and relationships that conforming data must satisfy. They enable validating RDF against application-specific requirements.

Constraints as shapes: Shapes group related constraints into reusable validation patterns. A 'Person shape' might require exactly one name, at least one email with proper format, an optional age between 0 and 150, and relationships only to organizations for employment. This shape defines what constitutes a valid person record.

Node shapes vs. property shapes: Node shapes define constraints on resources themselves—what type, what properties required. Property shapes define constraints on specific properties within node shapes—datatype, cardinality, allowed values. This two-level structure enables composing complex validations from simpler pieces.

Targets: Shapes specify which nodes they apply to through targets. A shape might target all instances of a particular class, nodes with certain property values, or explicitly listed individuals. Flexible targeting enables applying different validation rules to different parts of a dataset.

Validation reports: When data doesn't conform to shapes, SHACL validators generate detailed reports identifying which nodes violated which constraints. These machine-readable reports support automated quality gates, user feedback in data entry interfaces, and documentation of compliance issues.

Related: Node Shape and Property Shape are specific types. SHACL is the language. Constraint and Value Set define requirements. Validation is the category.

terms.name: Reasoning Concept
terms.description: semantic modeling process of deriving new facts or conclusions from existing knowledge using logical rules and inference.

terms.name: Distribution
terms.description: data asset that represents a specific accessible form of a dataset
terms.additionalInformation:
A Distribution is a specific available form of a dataset—a particular format, access method, or delivery mechanism through which the dataset can be accessed. Distributions represent how users actually obtain data: as file downloads (CSV, JSON, RDF), through APIs (REST, GraphQL), via query endpoints (SPARQL), or through other access methods. One dataset typically has multiple distributions serving different user needs.

Format diversity: Different users need different formats. Data scientists want CSV or Parquet for analysis. Web developers prefer JSON APIs. Semantic web applications need RDF. Rather than forcing one format, datasets offer multiple distributions—the same data packaged differently. Each distribution has format, access URL, size, and other technical metadata.

Access methods: Distributions vary by access method: direct download provides files for local processing, SPARQL endpoints enable remote querying without downloading, APIs support programmatic access with filtering and pagination, and data streams provide continuous or periodic updates. Each method suits different use cases and technical capabilities.

Example: A dataset of public transportation schedules might have distributions including: (1) a ZIP file containing CSV tables for download, (2) a JSON REST API for querying specific routes, (3) a GTFS feed for transit applications, (4) a SPARQL endpoint for semantic queries, and (5) an RDF/Turtle file for linked data applications. Same data, five distributions.

DCAT modeling: In DCAT vocabulary, distributions are linked to datasets via dcat:distribution property. Each distribution has dcat:accessURL for access, dcat:downloadURL if downloadable, dcat:mediaType for format, dcat:byteSize for size, and licensing information. This machine-readable metadata enables applications to programmatically select appropriate distributions.

Format negotiation: For linked data, content negotiation enables a single URL to serve multiple distributions transparently. Requesting a dataset URI with Accept: text/turtle returns Turtle, while Accept: application/ld+json returns JSON-LD. This provides multiple distributions through a unified interface.

Maintenance considerations: Each distribution requires maintenance—files must be updated when source data changes, APIs need monitoring and scaling, and endpoints require infrastructure. Organizations balance distribution variety against maintenance costs. Common practice provides a few well-chosen distributions covering major use cases rather than exhaustive options.

Related: Dataset is what distributions distribute. Serialization Formats determine distribution formats. SPARQL Endpoint is a distribution type. Content Negotiation enables multiple distributions. Access & Publication includes distributions.

terms.name: Dataset
terms.description: data asset representing a collection of data organized as a coherent whole, typically with metadata describing its content.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Dataset is a collection of data organized as a coherent whole, typically with metadata describing its content, provenance, structure, and access methods. In semantic contexts, datasets often contain RDF graphs, may be distributed across multiple serialization formats or endpoints, and are described using vocabularies like DCAT (Data Catalog Vocabulary) to support discovery and reuse.

More than files: A dataset is a conceptual entity—the data itself—separate from how it's distributed. The same dataset might be available as a CSV download, through a SPARQL endpoint, via an API, and as RDF dump files. Each access method is a distribution of the dataset, but the dataset as a whole is what users discover and reference.

Dataset metadata: Describing datasets with rich metadata enables discovery and assessment. Typical metadata includes title, description, publisher, creation date, update frequency, themes/topics, geographic coverage, temporal coverage, and license. Data catalogs aggregate this metadata, making datasets findable through search and browsing.

RDF datasets: In RDF, a dataset has specific technical meaning: a collection of named graphs plus an optional default graph. This structure enables organizing triples by provenance, version, or logical partition while keeping them within a single queryable entity. SPARQL queries can target specific graphs or query across the entire dataset.

Example: A government open data portal might have a 'Census Demographics' dataset with metadata describing what it contains, coverage areas, and update schedule. This dataset has distributions: CSV files for download, a SPARQL endpoint for queries, and JSON-LD for linked data. Users discover the dataset through metadata and choose appropriate distributions for their needs.

DCAT descriptions: The Data Catalog Vocabulary (DCAT) provides standard RDF properties for describing datasets, distributions, and catalogs. Using DCAT enables federated discovery—data catalogs can exchange dataset descriptions, and applications can discover datasets across multiple catalogs using uniform queries.

Versioning and evolution: Datasets evolve through versions as data updates. Good practice assigns version identifiers and preserves historical versions when possible. Metadata should indicate current version, update frequency, and relationships between versions. This enables reproducible analyses and tracking how data changes over time.

Related: Distribution provides access to datasets. Data Catalog organizes dataset metadata. Named Graph structures RDF datasets. DCAT vocabulary describes datasets. Access & Publication includes dataset concepts.

terms.name: Upper Ontology
terms.description: ontology that defines very general, domain-independent concepts like object, event, time, and space to provide a foundation for integration.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Upper Ontology (also called foundational or top-level ontology) defines very general, domain-independent concepts that are applicable across all fields of knowledge. These include fundamental categories like object, process, quality, time, space, and causation—concepts so basic they appear in virtually any domain model. Upper ontologies provide a foundation for integrating domain-specific ontologies by offering common high-level abstractions.

Why upper ontologies: Different domains often need to relate fundamental concepts—every domain has objects that change over time, participate in processes, have qualities, and exist in space. By aligning domain ontologies to a shared upper ontology, you create bridges for integration. If a biomedical ontology and a manufacturing ontology both extend the same upper ontology concepts, systems can reason about commonalities despite domain differences.

Major upper ontologies: BFO (Basic Formal Ontology) distinguishes continuants (things that endure through time) from occurrents (processes that unfold over time). DOLCE (Descriptive Ontology for Linguistic and Cognitive Engineering) focuses on cognitive and linguistic aspects. SUMO (Suggested Upper Merged Ontology) aims for comprehensive coverage. Each embodies different philosophical commitments about how to categorize reality.

Philosophical foundations: Upper ontologies engage with deep philosophical questions: Is a hole a thing? Are collections different from their members? Do processes have temporal parts? Different ontologies make different choices, and these choices affect how domain concepts are modeled. This philosophical depth makes upper ontologies powerful but also complex and sometimes controversial.

Practical adoption: Upper ontologies are most common in scientific domains where integration across fields is critical—biomedicine, environmental science, intelligence analysis. The Gene Ontology and many biological ontologies align with BFO. However, many enterprise and commercial knowledge graphs skip upper ontologies, finding them too abstract and complex for practical value relative to effort required.

Trade-offs: Using an upper ontology imposes structure and requires learning its categories and principles. This overhead pays off when integrating many domain ontologies or when formal precision matters. For single-domain applications or pragmatic knowledge graphs, the complexity often exceeds the benefit. As with many ontology decisions, the right choice depends on your integration requirements and philosophical tolerance.

Related: Domain Ontology and Application Ontology build on upper ontologies. Ontology general concept. Knowledge Representation broader context.

terms.name: broadMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is broader in meaning than another across different concept schemes.
terms.additionalInformation:
The skos:broadMatch property indicates that one concept in a SKOS scheme has a broader, more general meaning than another concept in a different scheme. BroadMatch enables hierarchical mapping across vocabularies, supporting navigation and translation between classification systems with different granularities.

Cross-scheme hierarchy: BroadMatch extends the broader/narrower hierarchy across concept schemes. If your internal category 'Python Programming' maps to an industry category 'Programming Languages,' that's a broadMatch—the industry category is more general, encompassing Python and other languages. This mapping preserves hierarchical relationships across vocabularies.

Versus broader: Use skos:broader for hierarchical relationships within a single concept scheme. Use skos:broadMatch for hierarchical relationships between concepts in different schemes. This distinction respects vocabulary boundaries while enabling cross-vocabulary reasoning.

Asymmetric relationship: BroadMatch has direction—if A broadMatch B, then B narrowMatch A (the inverse). One concept is more general, the other more specific. This asymmetry reflects real semantic relationships and supports navigation in both directions.

Mapping granularity: BroadMatch enables translating between fine-grained and coarse-grained classifications. Regulatory reporting might require mapping detailed internal product categories to broader standard industry categories. BroadMatch formalizes these up-the-hierarchy mappings.

Related: narrowMatch is the inverse. broader applies within schemes. exactMatch and closeMatch for equivalence. Linking & Alignment includes broadMatch.

terms.name: Annotation Property
terms.description: semantic property used to add metadata or documentation to model elements without affecting logical reasoning.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Annotation Property is a special kind of property used to add metadata, documentation, or labels to ontology elements without affecting logical reasoning. Annotation properties provide human-readable descriptions, version information, editorial notes, and other documentation that helps people understand and use the ontology but doesn't participate in inference or validation.

Documentation vs. inference: Standard properties affect reasoning—domain and range constrain types, property characteristics enable inference. Annotation properties explicitly don't participate in reasoning. They're for human consumption and tooling support. Reasoners ignore annotations when computing entailments, ensuring documentation doesn't create unintended logical consequences.

Standard annotations: RDFS and OWL define core annotation properties: rdfs:label provides human-readable names, rdfs:comment offers descriptions, rdfs:seeAlso links to related resources, rdfs:isDefinedBy indicates the defining vocabulary. owl:versionInfo tracks versions, owl:deprecated marks obsolete terms. These standard annotations enable basic documentation and tool support.

Multilingual labels: rdfs:label can provide names in multiple languages: :Person rdfs:label "Person"@en, "Personne"@fr, "Persona"@es. Tools and interfaces can display labels in user-preferred languages, making ontologies more accessible internationally. Comments and descriptions can similarly be multilingual.

Editorial workflow: Custom annotation properties support ontology development workflows: ex:editorialNote for curator comments, ex:proposedChange for suggested modifications, ex:sourceReference citing where definitions came from. These annotations help distributed teams coordinate ontology development and maintain quality.

Tool-specific annotations: Ontology editors and visualization tools use annotations for layout information, colors, display preferences, and other tool-specific data. These annotations enable round-tripping through tools without losing customizations, though they're typically not interoperable across different tools.

When to use: Use annotation properties for any information aimed at human users or tools rather than reasoning engines. Documentation, provenance, workflow status, and presentation information belong in annotations. Information that should affect reasoning or validation belongs in standard properties, classes, or restrictions.

Related: Property is the general concept. Object Property and Datatype Property affect reasoning. Ontology uses annotations for documentation. Model Elements includes annotation properties.

terms.name: T-Box
terms.description: knowledge representation component of a knowledge base that defines the vocabulary, classes, and properties.
terms.additionalInformation:
The T-Box (Terminological Box) is the schema layer of a knowledge base that defines the vocabulary, classes, properties, and rules of a domain. It represents the 'template' or 'model' that describes what kinds of things exist and how they can be related, without containing specific instances or data.

Conceptual separation: The T-Box vs A-Box distinction comes from Description Logic and helps separate concerns in knowledge engineering. The T-Box defines what can be said (the vocabulary and constraints), while the A-Box contains what is said (the actual facts). This separation enables reusing the same model across different datasets and validating instance data against schema definitions.

Example: A T-Box might define that Person is a class, hasAge is a datatype property with range xsd:integer, and Employee is a subclass of Person. These definitions don't describe any specific person—they establish the vocabulary and constraints.

Common use: When designing an ontology or data model, you're primarily working on the T-Box. Ontology engineers define classes, properties, domains, ranges, cardinality constraints, and logical axioms. Data architects map these to database schemas or validation rules.

In practice: The T-Box is typically smaller and more stable than the A-Box. You might have a T-Box with 100 classes and 200 properties, but an A-Box with millions of individuals. Changes to the T-Box often require migration or validation of existing instance data, so it evolves more slowly.

Why it matters: Understanding the T-Box/A-Box distinction helps when debugging data issues (is this a schema problem or a data problem?), when versioning ontologies (T-Box changes have broader impact), and when optimizing queries (T-Box reasoning happens once, A-Box queries happen repeatedly).

Related: A-Box is the complementary instance layer. Ontology and Schema are often synonymous with T-Box. Reasoning can operate on both T-Box (schema inference) and A-Box (instance classification).

terms.name: Min Cardinality
terms.description: cardinality constraint specifying the minimum number of values required for a property.
terms.additionalInformation:
Min Cardinality specifies the minimum number of values required for a property, enforcing that individuals must have at least N values. This constraint ensures mandatory properties are present and enables modeling requirements like 'every person must have at least one name' or 'a committee must have at least three members.'

Required properties: Minimum cardinality 1 makes a property required—individuals must have at least one value. This is common for essential attributes: people must have names, products must have prices, documents must have creation dates. The constraint ensures no required information is missing.

Multiple required values: Higher minimum cardinalities require multiple values. A triangle must have at least three vertices, a board of directors must have at least five members. These constraints enforce domain rules about quantities that must be satisfied.

OWL restrictions: OWL expresses minimum cardinality through class restrictions: 'Person with at least one email address' defines a class of people who have emails. Individuals without emails aren't members of this restricted class. This enables defining classes based on property counts.

SHACL validation: SHACL sh:minCount validates that actual data meets minimum requirements. If a person record has no name when name has minCount 1, that's a validation error. The report identifies which individuals and properties violate constraints, supporting data quality checking.

Inference vs. validation: OWL minimum cardinality supports reasoning—if something is stated to be in a class requiring at least N values, it must have at least N values (even if not visible). SHACL validates visible data—counting actual values and reporting when too few exist. Different paradigms serve different purposes.

Related: Max Cardinality limits values. Exact Cardinality specifies precise counts. Cardinality is the general concept. SHACL and Validation check minimum requirements.

terms.name: A-Box
terms.description: knowledge representation that contains the actual instance data and facts of a knowledge base, representing concrete individuals and their property values.
terms.additionalInformation:
The A-Box (Assertional Box) represents the instance data layer of a knowledge base—the actual facts, individuals, and property values that describe specific entities in your domain. While the T-Box defines what can be said, the A-Box contains what you actually say about particular things in the world.

Facts and assertions: A-Box statements make assertions about individuals: 'John Smith is 42 years old,' 'Tesla Inc. is headquartered in Austin,' 'Document #1234 was created on 2023-05-15.' These statements use the vocabulary defined in the T-Box but describe specific entities and their properties. In RDF terms, the A-Box consists of statements where the subject is an individual rather than a class or property.

Scale differences: While a T-Box might contain hundreds or thousands of classes and properties, an A-Box can contain millions or billions of individuals. A product ontology might define 50 classes, but a product catalog might contain 10 million product instances. This scale difference affects storage, querying, and reasoning strategies.

Example: Given a T-Box defining Person class and hasAge property, the A-Box might contain: :JohnSmith rdf:type :Person, :JohnSmith :hasAge 42, :JaneSmith rdf:type :Person, :JaneSmith :worksFor :AcmeCorp. Each statement describes a specific individual using the T-Box vocabulary.

Validation against schema: The T-Box defines constraints that A-Box data should satisfy. If the T-Box specifies that every Person must have exactly one birth date, validation checks each Person individual in the A-Box to ensure compliance. This separation enables evolving the schema and validating or migrating existing data accordingly.

Reasoning and classification: Reasoners use T-Box axioms to infer additional A-Box facts. If the T-Box states that Employees are Persons with employers, and the A-Box contains facts that John works for Acme Corp, a reasoner can infer that John is an Employee even if not explicitly stated. This A-Box reasoning enables deriving implicit knowledge from explicit facts.

Query focus: Most SPARQL queries target the A-Box—finding individuals matching certain patterns. T-Box queries might explore the schema structure, but the valuable operational queries discover products matching criteria, people with certain relationships, or events in time ranges—all A-Box questions.

Related: T-Box provides the schema. Individual and Named Individual are A-Box elements. Reasoning infers new A-Box facts. Validation checks A-Box conformance to T-Box.

terms.name: N-Triple
terms.description: serialization format that provides a line-based, plain-text format for RDF using full URIs.
terms.additionalInformation:
N-Triples is a line-based, plain-text format for RDF where each line represents exactly one triple using full URIs without abbreviations. Its extreme simplicity—one triple per line with no syntactic shortcuts—makes it ideal for streaming processing, parallel parsing, line-based text tools, and handling massive datasets where simplicity trumps readability.

Radically simple: N-Triples eliminates all syntactic complexity. Every line contains subject, predicate, and object separated by spaces, terminated with a period: <http://example.org/alice> <http://schema.org/name> "Alice" . No prefixes, no abbreviations, no multi-line structures—just pure triples. This simplicity enables trivial parsing and generation.

Streaming and tooling: Because N-Triples is line-based, standard Unix tools work perfectly: grep finds triples matching patterns, sort organizes data, uniq removes duplicates, split partitions large files, and wc -l counts triples. This enables processing billion-triple datasets with simple shell scripts rather than specialized RDF tools.

Example: A simple N-Triples file looks like: <http://example.org/alice> <http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#type> <http://schema.org/Person> . <http://example.org/alice> <http://schema.org/name> "Alice Smith" . <http://example.org/alice> <http://schema.org/age> "42"^^<http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#integer> . Verbose but unambiguous and easy to parse.

Parallelization: N-Triples files can be processed in parallel trivially—split the file into chunks at line boundaries, process each chunk independently, then merge results. No need to track context or parse complex structures. This enables massive-scale data processing with simple distributed systems.

Canonical representation: N-Triples provides a canonical form for RDF—a standard way to write any triple with no ambiguity. This supports diff/merge operations, cryptographic signing of datasets, and exact comparison. When precise reproducibility matters, N-Triples' lack of flexibility is an advantage.

Trade-offs: N-Triples sacrifices human readability and file size for parsing simplicity. Files are large and repetitive compared to Turtle. But for machine processing, data pipelines, and streaming scenarios, these trade-offs are worthwhile. Use N-Triples for processing, Turtle for human interaction.

Related: N-Quads extends N-Triples for named graphs. Turtle adds syntactic conveniences. Serialization Formats includes N-Triples. RDF is what N-Triples encodes. Dataset processing often uses N-Triples.

terms.name: Reflexive Property
terms.description: property characteristic where every individual relates to itself
terms.additionalInformation:
A Reflexive Property is one where every individual necessarily relates to itself. This characteristic formalizes self-relationships that hold universally. Common reflexive properties include sameAs, equalTo, or knows_of (everything knows of itself)—relationships where the self-connection is inherent in the property's meaning.

Universal self-relation: If a property is reflexive, then for every individual I, the triple 'I property I' holds automatically. A reasoner can infer these self-loops without explicit assertion. This is useful for properties where self-relationship is definitional—everything is equal to itself, everything is part of itself (in some part-whole definitions).

Limited practical use: Reflexivity is less commonly used than other property characteristics because truly universal self-relationships are rare in domain modeling. Most properties don't meaningfully apply from entities to themselves. Reflexivity appears mainly in mathematical or logical contexts—equality, equivalence, identity.

Identity properties: Properties like owl:sameAs are reflexive—every resource is identical to itself. This is part of what makes sameAs an equivalence relation (reflexive, symmetric, and transitive). Equivalence classes depend on reflexivity to include each element with itself.

Reflexivity with transitivity: Combining reflexive and transitive creates interesting patterns. If a property is reflexive and transitive, then chains of the property always include the endpoints relating to themselves. This affects reasoning about paths and closures in graphs.

Not common in data: Explicitly asserting reflexive triples (I relates to I) is rare because it's usually uninformative. If reflexivity is definitional, the reasoner infers it. If it's not, asserting it is strange. Most data models don't need or use reflexive properties beyond foundational identity/equality concepts.

Related: Irreflexive Property is the opposite. Property Characteristic is the category. sameAs is reflexive. Transitive Property often combines with reflexivity.

terms.name: Dereferencing
terms.description: data service for retrieving information about a resource by accessing its URI over HTTP, making URIs both identifiers and access points.
terms.additionalInformation:
Dereferencing is the process of retrieving information about a resource by accessing its URI over HTTP. It turns identifiers into active information access points—when you encounter a URI, you can dereference it to learn what it represents. This capability is fundamental to linked data, enabling discovery and navigation across distributed semantic datasets.

HTTP GET semantics: Dereferencing typically involves HTTP GET on a URI. If the URI is dereferenceable (follows linked data best practices), the server returns information about the identified resource—its properties, relationships, and documentation. This makes URIs simultaneously identifiers and documentation access mechanisms.

Discovery mechanism: Dereferencing enables discovering meaning dynamically. When processing data containing unfamiliar URIs, applications can dereference them to learn what they represent, what vocabulary they come from, and how they should be interpreted. This reduces need for offline vocabulary documentation.

Content negotiation: Dereferencing often uses content negotiation to serve appropriate formats. Browsers get HTML, semantic clients get RDF, APIs get JSON. The same dereferenceable URI serves multiple audiences without requiring separate addresses.

Challenges: Dereferencing adds latency—every unknown URI potentially triggers an HTTP request. It requires internet connectivity and assumes URIs remain accessible. Production systems often cache dereferenced content or use local mirrors rather than real-time dereferencing. Nevertheless, the capability is foundational to linked data architecture.

Related: URI and IRI are dereferenced. Content Negotiation determines representations. Linked Data relies on dereferencing. Access & Publication includes dereferencing.

terms.name: Class
terms.description: model element representing a category or type that groups individuals sharing common characteristics.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Class represents a category or type of things, grouping individuals that share common characteristics. In object-oriented terms, a class is like a template that defines what properties and relationships instances can have. In logical terms, a class is a set of individuals with shared attributes. Classes provide the categorical structure that organizes knowledge in semantic models.

Individuals and membership: Individuals are members of classes through the rdf:type property: :alice rdf:type :Person states that alice is an instance of the Person class. An individual can belong to multiple classes—someone might be both a Person and an Employee. This class membership enables querying by type: 'find all Persons' or 'find all Employees.'

Class hierarchies: Classes can be organized hierarchically using rdfs:subClassOf. If Employee is a subclass of Person, then all employees are automatically persons. This hierarchy enables reasoning—a query for Persons can return Employees without explicitly stating each employee is a person. Hierarchies structure knowledge from general to specific.

Intensional vs. extensional: Classes can be defined intensionally (by necessary and sufficient conditions) or extensionally (by listing members). An intensional definition might say 'Adult is a Person with age >= 18.' An extensional definition lists all adults. OWL enables intensional definitions through restrictions; SKOS and simpler models use extensional membership.

Open vs. closed classes: Under Open World Assumption, class membership is never complete—there might be additional members not yet known. This differs from database tables where the table contents represent all members. Reasoning about 'all members of a class' requires care—you're reasoning about all known members, not necessarily all actual members.

Metaclasses: Classes are themselves resources and can have properties: labels, descriptions, creation dates, versioning information. In RDFS/OWL, classes are instances of rdfs:Class or owl:Class. This meta-level modeling enables treating the schema itself as data.

Related: Individual instances belong to classes. SubClassOf creates hierarchies. Property has domain/range classes. T-Box defines classes. Model Elements includes classes.

terms.name: SPARQL
terms.description: query language and protocol that retrieves and manipulates RDF graph data, supporting pattern matching, filtering, aggregation, and federated queries across endpoints.
