A Classification Scheme is a system for categorizing items into predefined classes or categories, often using notation codes to represent the classifications. Unlike taxonomies which organize concepts, classification schemes focus on organizing physical or digital objects—books in libraries, products in catalogs, documents in archives—by assigning them to systematic categories.

Notation systems: Classification schemes typically use notation—numeric, alphabetic, or alphanumeric codes—to represent categories systematically. Dewey Decimal uses numbers (500 for Science, 510 for Mathematics). Library of Congress uses letters and numbers (QA for Mathematics). The notation encodes hierarchical position and enables systematic shelving or filing of items.

Enumerative vs. faceted: Enumerative classification schemes list all possible categories explicitly. The Dewey Decimal Classification enumerates thousands of categories spanning human knowledge. Faceted classification schemes define attributes (facets) that can be combined—a product might be classified by material + function + size. Faceted approaches offer more flexibility but require more sophisticated implementation.

Library classification: Major library classification schemes include Dewey Decimal Classification (DDC), Library of Congress Classification (LCC), and Universal Decimal Classification (UDC). These mature systems have evolved over more than a century to organize millions of books. Their hierarchical structure supports browsing—users exploring 500s find science books, 510s find mathematics within that.

Beyond libraries: Classification schemes apply broadly: medical coding systems like ICD-10 classify diagnoses and procedures, product classification schemes like HS Codes enable international trade statistics, patent classification systems organize technical disclosures. Each domain develops schemes reflecting its organizational needs and established practices.

RDF representation: SKOS can represent classification schemes using notation properties and hierarchical relationships. The classification codes become skos:notation values, and hierarchical relationships use skos:broader/narrower. This enables traditional classification schemes to participate in linked data ecosystems while maintaining their systematic notation.

Governance and standards: Established classification schemes have authoritative bodies maintaining them—OCLC for Dewey, Library of Congress for LCC, WHO for ICD. Updates balance stability (established categories support legacy data) with evolution (new knowledge areas need new categories). International standards enable cross-border consistency for trade, healthcare, and other domains.

Related: Taxonomy is conceptually similar. Controlled Vocabulary provides terms. SKOS enables RDF representation. Knowledge Organization Systems is the broader category.

terms.name: RDF
terms.description: standard for representing data as graphs of subject-predicate-object triples, providing a flexible model for describing resources and their relationships.
terms.additionalInformation:
RDF (Resource Description Framework) is the foundational standard for representing data as graphs of subject-predicate-object triples. It provides a flexible, extensible model for describing resources and their relationships, enabling data integration, linking, and exchange across organizational and system boundaries. RDF forms the base layer of semantic web technologies.

Data model: RDF defines an abstract graph model where resources (identified by URIs) are connected through typed relationships (properties) to other resources or literal values. This simple triple structure proves remarkably flexible—any kind of information can be expressed, from bibliographic metadata to scientific observations to business transactions.

Resource-centric: RDF centers on resources as first-class entities. Anything with identity—people, places, concepts, documents, organizations—is a resource that can be described and linked. This resource orientation differs from document-centric or record-centric models, enabling entity-focused integration.

Open world: RDF embraces the open world assumption—missing information is unknown, not false. Schemas are optional and flexible. New properties can be added without altering structures. This openness facilitates incremental development and integration of heterogeneous data sources.

Standards family: RDF is a family of specifications: the abstract model, serialization formats (Turtle, JSON-LD, RDF/XML), query language (SPARQL), schema vocabulary (RDFS), and related standards. Together they provide a complete stack for semantic data management.

Practical applications: RDF powers knowledge graphs, data catalogs, linked open data, scientific databases, and integration platforms. Its strength lies in connecting diverse data sources through shared vocabularies and identifiers, enabling queries and analytics that span system boundaries.

Related: Triple and RDF Graph are structural elements. RDFS and OWL extend RDF. SPARQL queries RDF. Serialization Formats encode RDF. Standards category includes RDF.

terms.name: Ontology Module
terms.description: ontology component that is self-contained and reusable, supporting modular design and distributed development.
terms.additionalInformation:
An Ontology Module is a self-contained, reusable component of a larger ontology that can be developed, maintained, versioned, and imported independently. Modularization addresses the challenge of managing large ontologies by breaking them into coherent pieces that can be composed as needed, much like software modules enable managing complex codebases.

Modularity benefits: Large monolithic ontologies become difficult to maintain, understand, and evolve. Different parts may have different update cycles, governance, or expertise requirements. Modules enable distributed development—different teams can work on different modules simultaneously. Users can import only relevant modules rather than the entire ontology, reducing complexity and improving performance.

Module boundaries: Effective modules have clear boundaries and minimal coupling. A large medical ontology might separate anatomy, diseases, treatments, and diagnostic procedures into modules. Each can be understood independently, though they reference each other through defined interfaces. Changes within a module don't affect other modules unless interfaces change.

Import mechanisms: OWL provides owl:imports for including one ontology within another. When Ontology A imports Module B, all of B's definitions become available in A. This enables composing complex ontologies from simpler pieces. Import management requires careful versioning—which version of each module does the application use?

Versioning strategies: Modules can be versioned independently. The anatomy module might be stable, updated annually, while the treatment module evolves monthly with new therapies. Applications specify which version of each module they depend on. This enables stability (modules don't unexpectedly change) while allowing evolution (new versions are available when ready).

Circular dependencies: Module design must avoid circular imports where A imports B and B imports A. This typically requires careful interface design with shared foundational modules that both import, or refactoring to extract common concepts into a third module. Dependency management tools can detect and warn about circular dependencies.

Extraction and reuse: Modularization enables extracting relevant subsets of large ontologies. If you need only drug concepts from a comprehensive medical ontology, you might import just the pharmacology module. Extraction algorithms can automatically identify minimal modules supporting specific concepts, enabling selective reuse.

Related: Ontology is what gets modularized. Namespace helps organize module identification. OWL imports mechanism. Domain Ontology and Upper Ontology often use modularization.

terms.name: Named Individual
terms.description: individual that is explicitly identified by a URI rather than an anonymous blank node, allowing it to be referenced or linked from other sources.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Named Individual is an instance that is explicitly identified by a URI, as opposed to an anonymous blank node. The URI provides global identity, enabling the individual to be referenced from other datasets, linked to external resources, and discovered through URI dereferencing. Named individuals are the foundation of linked data and knowledge graph integration.

Global identity: The URI <http://example.org/person/alice> uniquely identifies one individual across all systems. Any dataset using that URI refers to the same entity. This global identity is what enables the web of data—distributed datasets can reference common entities, creating a graph that spans organizational and system boundaries.

Dereferenceability: Best practice for named individuals is making their URIs dereferenceable—HTTP GET on the URI should return information about the individual. This enables discovery: when you encounter an unfamiliar URI in data, you can look it up to learn what it represents. Dereferencing turns identifiers into live access points for their descriptions.

Persistent identifiers: Named individuals should use persistent URIs that remain stable even as systems change. Organizations use PURL services, DOI systems, or dedicated identifier domains to ensure URIs don't break when websites are reorganized. Persistence is critical—broken URIs fracture the graph and break applications relying on those identifiers.

When to name individuals: Create named individuals for entities that need to be referenced externally, linked across datasets, or have independent existence worth preserving. People, organizations, published documents, places, and products typically merit named individuals. Intermediate objects or supporting data that matter only in local context can use blank nodes.

Identifier design: Good URIs are opaque (don't encode semantics), follow consistent patterns, and use hash or slash conventions appropriately. Avoid encoding information that might change—/person/12345 is better than /person/alice-smith-engineer because names and roles change but IDs remain stable.

Related: Individual is the general concept. Unnamed Individual is the anonymous alternative. URI provides the identifier. Dereferencing makes URIs actionable. Linking & Alignment connects named individuals.

terms.name: Max Cardinality
terms.description: cardinality constraint specifying the maximum number of values allowed for a property.
terms.additionalInformation:
Max Cardinality specifies the maximum number of values allowed for a property, enforcing that individuals can have at most N values. This constraint prevents duplication and ensures properties intended to be single-valued or limited in quantity don't accumulate excessive values.

Single-valued properties: Maximum cardinality 1 makes a property single-valued—each individual has at most one value. Birth dates, primary keys, unique identifiers, and singular relationships like 'biological mother' should have max cardinality 1. This prevents data quality issues from duplicated values.

Limited quantities: Higher maximum cardinalities limit but don't require uniqueness. A person might have at most two phone numbers in some model, a product at most five images. These constraints reflect domain limits on how many values make sense.

Functional properties: OWL functional property declaration is equivalent to max cardinality 1. Both express that at most one value is allowed. Functional is more common for global property characteristics; max cardinality restrictions can apply conditionally to specific classes.

SHACL validation: SHACL sh:maxCount validates that data doesn't exceed limits. If a person has three values for a property with maxCount 2, that's a validation error. This catches data quality issues like duplicate entries or overly populated fields.

OWL reasoning: In OWL, exceeding max cardinality doesn't create an error—it triggers inference that the values must actually be identical (if functional) or creates an inconsistency. This reasoning behavior differs from validation's error reporting.

Related: Min Cardinality requires values. Exact Cardinality specifies precise counts. Functional Property implies max 1. Cardinality is the general concept. Validation checks maximums.

terms.name: Quad
terms.description: graph concept that extends a triple with a fourth element specifying the named graph it belongs to.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Quad extends a triple by adding a fourth element that identifies which named graph the statement belongs to. This enables managing multiple graphs within a single RDF dataset, tracking data provenance, implementing access control, and representing versioned or temporal data while maintaining the fundamental triple structure for describing resources.

Fourth element: A quad has the structure: subject, predicate, object, graph. The first three elements form a normal triple describing a fact. The fourth element—a URI identifying a named graph—indicates the context or source of that fact. Multiple quads can share the same subject-predicate-object while belonging to different graphs.

Provenance representation: Quads enable tracking where each statement came from. Triples from System A go in graph <http://example.org/graphs/systemA>, triples from System B in <http://example.org/graphs/systemB>. When analyzing integrated data, you can see which source contributed each fact, supporting trust assessments and data quality management.

Temporal versioning: Quads support temporal or versioned data by using different graphs for different time periods or versions. Facts valid in 2023 go in the 2023 graph, facts valid in 2024 in the 2024 graph. Queries can target specific time periods or compare across periods, all within a single dataset.

Serialization formats: N-Quads and TriG formats explicitly represent quads. N-Quads adds the graph URI as a fourth element on each line. TriG groups triples by graph in blocks. These formats enable exchanging datasets with named graphs, preserving the quad structure across systems.

SPARQL querying: SPARQL's GRAPH keyword enables querying across named graphs. Queries can specify which graph to search, bind the graph URI to variables for filtering, or aggregate results by source graph. This makes the fourth element queryable just like subject, predicate, or object.

Implementation considerations: Triplestores supporting named graphs typically implement them as quads internally, though they may present graph-oriented APIs. Indexes include the graph element for efficient filtering. The storage overhead of the fourth element is offset by the organizational and governance benefits when managing large diverse datasets.

Related: Triple is the basic unit. Named Graph provides the graph context. N-Quads and TriG serialize quads. RDF Graph is extended by this model.

terms.name: Value Set
terms.description: validation mechanism representing a defined collection of allowed values for a property.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Value Set is a defined collection of allowed values for a property or field, constraining choices to an enumerated list or specific range. Value sets enforce that data uses controlled terminology, valid codes, or acceptable ranges, supporting data quality and enabling meaningful aggregation.

Enumerated values: Value sets often list specific allowed values: status must be 'pending,' 'approved,' or 'rejected'; country codes from ISO 3166; product categories from an approved taxonomy. These closed lists ensure consistency and prevent invalid or non-standard values.

SHACL value sets: SHACL sh:in constraint specifies enumerated value sets: sh:in ("red" "green" "blue"). Values must be one of the listed options. This validates against controlled vocabularies or fixed enumerations.

Range constraints: Value sets can specify ranges for numeric or temporal values: age between 0 and 150, dates in the past, amounts greater than zero. SHACL provides sh:minInclusive, sh:maxInclusive, and related constraints for range validation.

Related: Controlled Vocabulary provides value sets. Constraint is the general concept. Validation checks against value sets. SHACL expresses value set constraints.

terms.name: Vocabulary
terms.description: knowledge organization system that collects terms and their definitions used within a particular domain or application.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Vocabulary is a collection of terms and their definitions used within a particular domain or application. In semantic web contexts, vocabularies define the classes and properties that can be used to describe resources, essentially providing the language for expressing information in RDF. Vocabularies range from small application-specific term sets to large standard vocabularies used globally.

RDF vocabularies: RDF vocabularies define terms (classes and properties) using RDFS or OWL. Dublin Core defines properties for describing publications (title, creator, date). FOAF (Friend of a Friend) defines classes and properties for describing people and social networks. Schema.org provides a comprehensive vocabulary for web content markup. These vocabularies enable consistent description across applications and datasets.

Namespace and terms: Each vocabulary has a namespace URI that groups its terms. Dublin Core uses http://purl.org/dc/terms/, FOAF uses http://xmlns.com/foaf/0.1/. Terms are identified by combining the namespace with a local name: dcterms:title, foaf:Person. This namespacing prevents conflicts when vocabularies define similar terms.

Reuse over reinvention: A core principle of semantic web best practices is reusing existing vocabularies rather than creating new ones. If Dublin Core already defines 'title,' use dcterms:title instead of inventing your own title property. Reuse enables interoperability—other systems understand standard vocabularies and can process data without custom mapping.

Vocabulary documentation: Good vocabularies include rich documentation: formal definitions in RDFS or OWL, human-readable descriptions and usage guidelines, examples showing how to use terms, and information about governance and versioning. This documentation helps users apply terms correctly and consistently.

Domain vs. general vocabularies: Some vocabularies aim for broad applicability—Dublin Core for any publications, FOAF for any people. Others target specific domains—FIBO for finance, SNOMED CT for clinical medicine. Applications typically use a mix: general vocabularies for common concepts, domain vocabularies for specialized knowledge, custom vocabularies only when necessary.

Vocabulary vs. ontology: The terms overlap but connote different emphasis. 'Vocabulary' suggests a practical collection of terms for describing data. 'Ontology' suggests formal logical definitions and reasoning capabilities. The same resource might be called either depending on context—is it primarily serving as terminology or as formal knowledge representation?

Related: RDFS and OWL define vocabulary terms. Controlled Vocabulary is similar in KOS context. Namespace organizes vocabulary terms. Schema and Ontology are more structured.

terms.name: Graph Store
terms.description: graph storage for managing and storing graph data, including CRUD operations.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Graph Store is a system for managing and storing graph data, including capabilities for creating, reading, updating, and deleting graphs. Graph stores may support RDF graphs, property graphs, or both, providing storage, indexing, query processing, and graph operations optimized for network-structured data.

Graph storage models: Graph stores can implement RDF triples with subject-predicate-object structure, property graphs with attributed nodes and edges, or hybrid models supporting both. The choice affects query capabilities, schema flexibility, and performance characteristics.

Beyond simple storage: Graph stores provide more than persistence—they offer transaction management, concurrency control, query optimization, indexing strategies, backup and recovery, replication, and access control. These enterprise features enable production deployments at scale.

CRUD operations: Graph stores support full CRUD lifecycle: creating new graphs or adding nodes/edges, reading through queries or traversals, updating existing data, and deleting graphs or elements. APIs may be graph-oriented (add this edge) or data-oriented (insert these triples).

Related: Triplestore is an RDF-specific graph store. RDF Graph and Property Graph are stored. Named Graph support enables organizing data. Access & Publication includes graph stores.

terms.name: Concept Scheme
terms.description: knowledge organization system that organizes concepts by semantic relationships, typically defined in SKOS to represent a set of interrelated ideas.
terms.additionalInformation:
A Concept Scheme is a collection of concepts organized by semantic relationships, representing a knowledge organization system as a coherent whole. In SKOS terminology, a concept scheme is the container for a taxonomy, thesaurus, classification, or controlled vocabulary, grouping related concepts together and providing metadata about the scheme itself.

SKOS concept schemes: SKOS uses skos:ConceptScheme to represent the overall knowledge organization system. Individual concepts belong to schemes via skos:inScheme properties. This enables representing multiple taxonomies or thesauri in a single RDF dataset while keeping them logically separate. A system might contain both a product taxonomy and a geographic taxonomy as distinct concept schemes.

Scheme metadata: Concept schemes carry metadata about the knowledge organization system: title, description, publisher, version, license, creation date, and coverage. This documentation helps users understand the scheme's scope, authority, and appropriate use. When selecting among multiple available schemes for the same domain, metadata informs the choice.

Top concepts: Concept schemes identify their top-level or entry-point concepts using skos:hasTopConcept. These root concepts provide starting points for navigation and help users understand the scheme's overall structure. For a product taxonomy, top concepts might be major product categories; for a subject thesaurus, broad topical areas.

Multiple schemes in datasets: RDF datasets often contain or reference multiple concept schemes. A data catalog might use Library of Congress Subject Headings for topics, ISO 3166 for countries, and a custom scheme for internal departments. Identifying which scheme each concept belongs to prevents confusion and enables appropriate processing of each.

Versioning and evolution: Publishing concept schemes as discrete RDF resources with URIs enables versioning. Version 1.0 of a taxonomy is a distinct resource from version 2.0, with its own URI and metadata. Applications can specify which version they're using, and migration tools can map between versions when concepts are added, merged, or deprecated.

Alignment across schemes: When multiple concept schemes cover similar domains, SKOS mapping properties (exactMatch, closeMatch, broadMatch, etc.) can link equivalent or related concepts across schemes. This enables translating between schemes—mapping your internal product categories to an industry standard classification, or linking national subject headings to Library of Congress headings.

Related: SKOS defines concept schemes. Taxonomy, Thesaurus, Classification Scheme are implemented as concept schemes. Knowledge Organization Systems is the abstract category.

terms.name: URI
terms.description: semantic resource identifier that provides a globally unique string for identifying a resource.
terms.additionalInformation:
A URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) is a string that globally identifies a resource using a standardized format. URIs provide the foundation for web-based identification, enabling resources to be referenced consistently across systems and organizations without central coordination. They're the fundamental identifier mechanism in RDF and the semantic web.

Global identification: Unlike database keys that are meaningful only within one system, URIs are globally unique. http://example.org/person/alice identifies Alice anywhere in the world. This global scope enables distributed data to reference common entities without namespace collisions or identifier conflicts.

Syntax and structure: URIs follow standard syntax: scheme (http, https, urn), authority (domain), path, optional query and fragment. The structure enables parsing, validation, and understanding of identifier components. HTTP URIs leverage existing web infrastructure for resolution.

URLs vs. URIs: URLs (Uniform Resource Locators) are URIs that can be resolved to retrieve resources—they're network addresses. URIs are more general—they identify things without necessarily providing access mechanisms. In practice, most RDF uses HTTP URIs, which are both identifiers and potentially resolvable URLs.

Dereferenceable URIs: Best practice makes URIs dereferenceable—performing HTTP GET should return information about the identified resource. This turns identifiers into active access points, enabling discovery and documentation. Dereferencing supports the linked data vision of a web of data.

Opacity principle: Good URIs are opaque—they don't encode semantics in their structure. /person/12345 is better than /person/alice-smith-engineer because names and roles change but IDs remain stable. Opacity supports persistence when attributes change.

Related: IRI extends URIs for internationalization. CURIE provides compact notation. Identifiers & Namespaces is the category. Dereferencing makes URIs actionable. Subject, Predicate, Object use URIs.

terms.name: SHACL
terms.description: standard language for validating RDF graphs against a set of conditions defined as shapes.
terms.additionalInformation:
SHACL (Shapes Constraint Language) is a W3C standard for validating RDF data against defined shapes and constraints. It enables expressing requirements like required properties, allowed datatypes, cardinality limits, value patterns, and complex business rules in a declarative, machine-processable format that validation engines can execute.

Validation focus: Unlike OWL which focuses on reasoning and inference, SHACL focuses on validation and quality checking. It defines what valid data should look like and reports violations when actual data doesn't conform. This closed-world validation complements open-world reasoning.

Shapes as requirements: SHACL shapes group related constraints into reusable patterns. A shape defines requirements for a class of resources: required properties, cardinality, datatypes, allowed values, patterns, and relationships. Shapes document data requirements and enable automated checking.

Validation reports: SHACL validators produce detailed reports when data violates constraints. Reports identify which resources violated which constraints, with severity levels and explanatory messages. This actionable feedback supports data quality workflows, user interface validation, and conformance testing.

SHACL-SPARQL: Beyond declarative constraint components, SHACL supports SPARQL-based constraints for complex business rules that can't be expressed through standard components. This extensibility enables expressing arbitrary requirements while maintaining machine-processability.

Practical applications: Organizations use SHACL for validating data before loading into triplestores, checking API inputs, documenting application profiles, generating data entry forms with validation, and demonstrating regulatory compliance.

Related: Shape, Node Shape, Property Shape are SHACL constructs. Constraint and Value Set define requirements. Validation is enabled by SHACL. Standards includes SHACL.

terms.name: Model Element
terms.description: semantic modeling component used to construct models, including classes, properties, individuals, and constraints.
terms.additionalInformation:
Model Elements are the building blocks used to construct semantic models and ontologies. They include classes that categorize entities, properties that describe attributes and relationships, individuals that represent specific instances, and various constraints that govern how these elements can be combined. Understanding these elements is essential for reading, creating, or maintaining any semantic model.

Classes as categories: Classes represent categories or types of things in a domain. A Person class represents the category of all people, while Organization represents companies, agencies, and institutions. Classes can be arranged hierarchically through subclass relationships, creating taxonomies from general to specific concepts. This hierarchy enables inheritance—subclasses inherit properties and constraints from their parents.

Properties as relationships: Properties define what can be said about classes and individuals. Object properties link resources to other resources (worksFor connecting a person to an organization), while datatype properties link resources to literal values (age with an integer). Properties themselves have characteristics—they can be transitive, symmetric, functional, or inverse, each affecting how reasoners process them.

Individuals as instances: While classes and properties define the schema, individuals represent actual entities in the domain. JohnSmith might be an individual of class Person. Named individuals have explicit URIs and can be referenced globally, while anonymous individuals (blank nodes) exist only in local context.

Constraints and restrictions: Model elements include various ways to constrain valid data. Domain and range specify what classes a property applies to and what values it can have. Cardinality constraints specify how many values are required or allowed. Restrictions define conditions for class membership based on property values. These constraints enable validation and reasoning.

Class expressions: Advanced modeling uses class expressions to define complex conditions. SubClassOf creates hierarchies, EquivalentClass defines synonymous classes, DisjointClasses ensures no overlap. These logical operations enable precise definitions and support automated reasoning about class membership and relationships.

Practical modeling: Building a semantic model involves identifying domain classes, defining their properties and relationships, specifying constraints that reflect business rules, and creating individuals to represent actual data. The richness of model elements available enables capturing complex domain knowledge formally, but modelers must balance expressiveness with maintainability and performance.

Related: Class, Property, and Individual are fundamental. Domain, Range, and Cardinality define constraints. Property Characteristic adds logical features. Restriction and class expressions provide advanced capabilities.

terms.name: Constraint
terms.description: validation mechanism representing a rule or condition that data must satisfy
terms.additionalInformation:
A Constraint is a rule or condition that data must satisfy to be considered valid. In RDF validation contexts like SHACL, constraints specify requirements on values, structures, and relationships that enable checking data quality, enforcing business rules, and ensuring conformance to specifications.

Types of constraints: Constraints vary widely: datatype constraints (must be integer), cardinality constraints (exactly one value), value constraints (from specific enumeration), pattern constraints (match regex), relationship constraints (only link to valid targets), uniqueness constraints (no duplicates), and logical constraints (if-then rules).

Validation vs. inference: Constraints in validation (SHACL) check whether data satisfies conditions, reporting violations. Constraints in ontologies (OWL) define necessary or sufficient conditions that enable classification and reasoning. The same constraint—'age must be non-negative'—serves different purposes in different paradigms.

Business rules: Constraints formalize business rules in machine-executable form. 'Invoices must have customer references,' 'Products must have prices,' 'Employees must be at least 18 years old'—these business requirements become constraints that automated systems can check and enforce.

Related: Cardinality, Domain, Range are specific constraint types. Shape and Property Shape contain constraints. Validation uses constraints. SHACL expresses constraints.

terms.name: exactMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts have the same meaning and can be used interchangeably across different schemes.
terms.additionalInformation:
The skos:exactMatch property indicates that two concepts from different SKOS concept schemes have the same meaning and can be used interchangeably in most applications. While similar to owl:sameAs, exactMatch is specifically designed for concept-level alignment and is weaker—it indicates semantic equivalence without the full logical implications of identity.

Cross-scheme alignment: ExactMatch links equivalent concepts across different taxonomies, thesauri, or controlled vocabularies. If your internal product category 'Software Applications' has the same meaning as an industry standard category with that name, exactMatch formalizes this equivalence. Applications can use either vocabulary, translating between them via the mapping.

Weaker than sameAs: Unlike owl:sameAs which makes strong identity claims, exactMatch acknowledges that the concepts belong to different schemes with potentially different governance and scope. The concepts are equivalent for practical purposes but remain distinct resources. This respects vocabulary independence while enabling alignment.

Symmetric and transitive: Like sameAs, exactMatch is symmetric (if A exactMatch B, then B exactMatch A) and transitive (if A exactMatch B and B exactMatch C, then A exactMatch C). These properties enable building equivalence networks across multiple concept schemes.

Usage guidelines: Use exactMatch when concepts have the same or highly overlapping meaning across schemes but you want to preserve their separate identities. It's appropriate for aligning subject headings, product categories, or topical classifications where equivalence is clear but vocabularies remain independent.

Related: closeMatch for near-equivalence. broadMatch and narrowMatch for hierarchical cross-scheme relationships. sameAs for full identity. Linking & Alignment category includes exactMatch.

terms.name: Value
terms.description: semantic modeling component representing the concrete data content assigned to properties, including literals and language-tagged strings.
terms.additionalInformation:
Values represent the concrete data content in semantic models—the actual numbers, strings, dates, and other literal information that properties carry. While URIs and blank nodes identify resources and create the graph structure, literals provide the leaves of the graph: the descriptive content, measurements, and facts that give meaning to the relationships.

Literals vs. resources: RDF makes a fundamental distinction between resources (identified by URIs or blank nodes) and literal values (concrete data). Resources can be subjects and objects of triples, serving as connection points in the graph. Literals can only be objects—they're endpoints that don't link further. This distinction reflects that you describe resources but you directly represent data.

Datatypes provide interpretation: A literal value like '42' has no inherent meaning until you specify its datatype. As xsd:integer it's a number for arithmetic. As xsd:string it's text. As xsd:hexBinary it's a byte sequence. RDF uses XML Schema datatypes as the standard type system, covering integers, decimals, booleans, dates, times, durations, and more. Correct datatypes ensure proper comparison, sorting, and validation.

Language tags for multilingual content: String literals can carry language tags indicating the natural language of the text: "Hello"@en, "Bonjour"@fr, "こんにちは"@ja. This enables representing the same property in multiple languages within a single dataset. Applications can select values matching user language preferences, supporting internationalization without separate data models.

String normalization challenges: Unlike databases with fixed string lengths and collations, RDF literals can contain arbitrary Unicode text. Case sensitivity, normalization forms, and cultural sorting rules vary across languages. SPARQL provides string functions but comparing and matching across writing systems requires careful attention to normalization and equivalence rules.

Custom datatypes: Beyond built-in XML Schema types, applications can define custom datatypes for domain-specific values. Geographic coordinates, chemical formulas, or proprietary encodings can be represented as custom datatypes with defined value spaces and comparison semantics. However, custom types reduce interoperability—other systems may not understand how to interpret or validate them.

Practical considerations: Choose appropriate datatypes to enable meaningful operations—use numeric types for values you'll do math on, date/time types for temporal reasoning, boolean for flags. Language-tag string properties for human-readable content that needs translation. Document datatype choices in ontologies and application profiles so data consumers know how to interpret and validate values.

Related: Literal is the general concept. Datatype specifies interpretation. Language Tag enables multilingual content. Datatype Property links resources to literals.

terms.name: Reification
terms.description: graph concept technique for making statements about statements by treating a triple as a resource.
terms.additionalInformation:
Reification is a technique for making statements about statements by treating a triple as a resource with its own properties. It enables expressing metadata like certainty, provenance, time validity, or supporting evidence for individual facts—saying not just that something is true, but when it became true, who said it, or how confident we are.

Why make statements about statements: Sometimes you need to qualify or contextualize individual facts. You might know that 'Alice works for Company X' but need to record when this employment started, which document states it, or that it's uncertain. Basic triples can't carry this metadata—you need a way to refer to the triple itself and make additional statements about it.

RDF reification vocabulary: RDF defines rdf:Statement class with properties rdf:subject, rdf:predicate, rdf:object to represent triples as resources. To reify 'Alice works for Company X,' you create a statement resource and assert its subject is Alice, its predicate is worksFor, and its object is Company X. Then you can add properties like ex:validFrom to this statement resource.

Verbosity problem: RDF reification is extremely verbose—representing one triple requires four additional triples (typing the statement and declaring its three components). This quadruples data size and complicates queries. For these reasons, RDF reification is rarely used in practice despite being formally defined in the standard.

Alternative patterns: Various workarounds evolved: creating intermediate nodes for relationships (employment events), using named graphs for provenance (each source gets its own graph), or using singleton properties (unique property instances). Each has trade-offs between expressiveness, query complexity, and data size.

N-ary relationships: Many reification use cases actually represent n-ary relationships—relationships involving more than two participants or having multiple aspects. Instead of reifying, consider modeling the relationship as a resource with properties. An 'Employment' resource can have properties for employee, employer, startDate, salary, etc. This is often clearer than reification.

RDF-star solution: RDF-star (being standardized as RDF 1.2) addresses reification's problems by allowing triples as subjects or objects of other triples: << Alice worksFor CompanyX >> validFrom "2023-01-01". This provides reification's expressiveness without the verbosity, and is likely to replace traditional reification approaches.

Related: RDF-star is the modern solution. Triple is what gets reified. Named Graph is an alternative for some use cases. Graph Fundamentals is the broader context.

terms.name: A-Box
terms.description: knowledge representation that contains the actual instance data and facts of a knowledge base, representing concrete individuals and their property values.

terms.name: Annotation Property
terms.description: semantic property used to add metadata or documentation to model elements without affecting logical reasoning.

terms.name: Application Ontology

terms.description: knowledge representation that combines and constrains elements from multiple vocabularies to meet specific needs.

terms.name: Asymmetric Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if A relates to B, then B cannot relate to A

terms.name: Authority File
terms.description: knowledge organization system that provides a curated list of authorized forms of names or terms to ensure consistency.

terms.name: Blank Node
terms.description: naming concept representing an anonymous resource without a global ID.

terms.name: CURIE
terms.description: naming concept for a compact URI that uses a prefix and local name separated by a colon.

terms.name: Cardinality
terms.description: model element representing a constraint on the number of values a property can have for an individual.

terms.name: Class
terms.description: model element representing a category or type that groups individuals sharing common characteristics.

terms.name: Classification Scheme
terms.description: knowledge organization system used for categorizing items into predefined classes, often using notation codes.

terms.name: Closed World Assumption
terms.description: reasoning concept where any statement not known to be true is assumed to be false.

terms.name: Concept Scheme
terms.description: knowledge organization system that organizes concepts by semantic relationships, typically defined in SKOS to represent a set of interrelated ideas.

terms.name: Constraint
terms.description: validation mechanism representing a rule or condition that data must satisfy

terms.name: Content Negotiation
terms.description: data service where clients and servers negotiate the format and language of resources.

terms.name: Context Graph
terms.description: graph concept used to enhance LLMs by organizing information as interconnected entities.

terms.name: Controlled Vocabulary
terms.description: knowledge organization system that provides an organized list of terms with defined meanings used consistently to tag or describe content.

terms.name: Data Asset
terms.description: semantic modeling component representing an organized collection of data that is published, shared, or managed as a discrete unit.

terms.name: Data Model
terms.description: knowledge representation that describes how data is organized, including entities, attributes, and relationships.

terms.name: Data Service
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing the method and technology for making semantic data available to users and applications, encompassing storage systems, query interfaces, and protocols.

terms.name: Dataset
terms.description: data asset representing a collection of data organized as a coherent whole, typically with metadata describing its content.

terms.name: Datatype
terms.description: value specification of how literal values should be interpreted and compared

terms.name: Datatype Property
terms.description: semantic property whose values are literals with datatypes, representing attributes like strings, numbers, or dates.

terms.name: Dereferencing
terms.description: data service for retrieving information about a resource by accessing its URI over HTTP, making URIs both identifiers and access points.

terms.name: DisjointClass
terms.description: model element constraint stating that two or more classes have no members in common.

terms.name: Distribution
terms.description: data asset that represents a specific accessible form of a dataset

terms.name: Domain
terms.description: class or classes whose members can have a particular property, specifying the types of things the property applies to.

terms.name: Domain Ontology
terms.description: ontology that models concepts and relationships specific to a particular field or area of knowledge.

terms.name: Entailment
terms.description: reasoning concept where one set of statements necessarily implies another, meaning the latter must be true if the former is.

terms.name: EquivalentClass
terms.description: model element relationship indicating that two classes have exactly the same members.

terms.name: Exact Cardinality
terms.description: cardinality constraint specifying exactly how many values a property must have.

terms.name: Functional Property
terms.description: property characteristic that can have at most one value for any given individual.

terms.name: Graph
terms.description: graph concept consisting of nodes connected by edges.

terms.name: Graph Concept
terms.description: semantic modeling building block representing the core concepts of graph-based data models.

terms.name: Graph Representation
terms.description: graph concept that provides a specific method for encoding or modeling graph-based data.

terms.name: Graph Storage
terms.description: graph concept for storing and managing graph data.

terms.name: Graph Store
terms.description: graph storage for managing and storing graph data, including CRUD operations.

terms.name: Graph Structure
terms.description: graph that organizes semantic data into a specific architectural pattern or network.

terms.name: IRI
terms.description: semantic resource identifier that extends URIs to support characters from all languages and scripts.

terms.name: Individual
terms.description: model element representing a specific instance or member of a class in the domain.

terms.name: Inference
terms.description: reasoning concept of deriving new triples from existing data using logical rules and axioms.

terms.name: Inverse Functional Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if two individuals share the same value, they must be the same individual.

terms.name: Inverse Property
terms.description: property characteristic that represents the reverse direction of another property.

terms.name: Irreflexive Property
terms.description: property characteristic where no individual can relate to itself.

terms.name: JSON-LD
terms.description: serialization format for linked data that embeds RDF in JSON using a context to define term meanings.

terms.name: Knowledge Graph
terms.description: paradigm of a network of interconnected entities and their relationships, often combining data from multiple sources.

terms.name: Knowledge Organization System
terms.description: semantic modeling component that provides a structured framework for organizing and categorizing information.

terms.name: Knowledge Representation
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing a formal system for encoding knowledge about a domain.

terms.name: Language Tag
terms.description: value code attached to a string literal that indicates the natural language of the text.

terms.name: Linked Data
terms.description: paradigm for publishing structured data on the web using standard formats and dereferenceable URIs.

terms.name: Linking Mechanism
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing the technique and property for connecting related concepts across different vocabularies, ontologies, or datasets to enable data integration.

terms.name: Linking Property
terms.description: linking mechanism used to establish correspondences between concepts across different schemes.

terms.name: Literal
terms.description: value representing concrete data rather than a reference to a resource.

terms.name: Mapping
terms.description: linking mechanism result of establishing correspondences between concepts, terms, or schemas across different systems.

terms.name: Max Cardinality
terms.description: cardinality constraint specifying the maximum number of values allowed for a property.

terms.name: Min Cardinality
terms.description: cardinality constraint specifying the minimum number of values required for a property.

terms.name: Model Element
terms.description: semantic modeling component used to construct models, including classes, properties, individuals, and constraints.

terms.name: N-Quad
terms.description: serialization format that extends N-Triples with a fourth element for the graph name.

terms.name: N-Triple
terms.description: serialization format that provides a line-based, plain-text format for RDF using full URIs.

terms.name: Named Graph
terms.description: graph structure identified by a URI, allowing metadata about the graph

terms.name: Named Individual
terms.description: individual that is explicitly identified by a URI rather than an anonymous blank node, allowing it to be referenced or linked from other sources.

terms.name: Namespace
terms.description: naming concept base IRI that groups related terms together and prevents naming conflicts.

terms.name: Naming Concept
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing a system for uniquely identifying and organizing resources on the web and in semantic models, including URIs and namespaces.

terms.name: Node Shape
terms.description: shape that defines constraints on nodes in a graph and validates individual resources.

terms.name: OWL
terms.description: standard semantic markup language for creating complex ontologies with logical axioms and constraints.

terms.name: Object
terms.description: triple component that provides the value or target of a relationship, which can be a URI, blank node, or literal.

terms.name: Object Property
terms.description: semantic property whose values are other resources or individuals, representing relationships between entities.

terms.name: Ontology
terms.description: knowledge representation that provides a formal, explicit specification of a shared conceptualization within a domain.

terms.name: Ontology Module
terms.description: ontology component that is self-contained and reusable, supporting modular design and distributed development.

terms.name: Open World Assumption
terms.description: reasoning concept where the absence of a statement does not mean it is false, only that it is unknown.

terms.name: Paradigm
terms.description: semantic modeling component encompassing the collection of methodologies, frameworks, and communities that apply semantic technologies.

terms.name: Predicate
terms.description: triple element that specifies the property or relationship being asserted between a subject and an object.

terms.name: Prefix
terms.description: naming concept that maps to a full namespace IRI to make IRIs more readable.

terms.name: Property
terms.description: model element that defines a relationship or attribute connecting resources or assigning values.

terms.name: Property Characteristic
terms.description: model element that defines a logical feature of how a property behaves

terms.name: Property Graph
terms.description: graph concept where both nodes and edges can have properties, often used in graph databases.

terms.name: Property Shape
terms.description: shape that defines constraints on specific properties within a node shape.

terms.name: Quad
terms.description: graph concept that extends a triple with a fourth element specifying the named graph it belongs to.

terms.name: Query Language
terms.description: standard that defines a formal syntax and protocol for retrieving and manipulating structured data.

terms.name: RDF
terms.description: standard for representing data as graphs of subject-predicate-object triples, providing a flexible model for describing resources and their relationships.

terms.name: RDF-star
terms.description: graph representation that provides an efficient way to make statements about statements.

terms.name: RDFS
terms.description: standard vocabulary extension to RDF that adds basic modeling primitives like classes and properties.

terms.name: RDF/XML
terms.description: serialization format that uses XML to encode RDF data.

terms.name: RDF Graph
terms.description: graph structure consisting of a set of RDF triples that together describe resources and their relationships.

terms.name: Range
terms.description: model element specifying the class, datatype, or set of values that a property can have.

terms.name: Reasoner
terms.description: reasoning concept component that performs logical inference over semantic data using rules and axioms.

terms.name: Reasoning Concept
terms.description: semantic modeling process of deriving new facts or conclusions from existing knowledge using logical rules and inference.

terms.name: Reflexive Property
terms.description: property characteristic where every individual relates to itself

terms.name: Reification
terms.description: graph concept technique for making statements about statements by treating a triple as a resource.

terms.name: Restriction
terms.description: model element class expression that describes individuals based on their property values.

terms.name: SHACL
terms.description: standard language for validating RDF graphs against a set of conditions defined as shapes.

terms.name: SKOS
terms.description: standard for representing taxonomies, thesauri, and classification schemes in RDF.

terms.name: SPARQL
terms.description: query language and protocol that retrieves and manipulates RDF graph data, supporting pattern matching, filtering, aggregation, and federated queries across endpoints.

terms.name: SPARQL Endpoint
terms.description: data service that accepts SPARQL queries over HTTP and returns results.

terms.name: Schema
terms.description: knowledge representation that provides a lightweight definition of the structure and constraints of data.

terms.name: Semantic Modeling
terms.description: model development practice of creating explicit, machine-readable representations of knowledge that capture meaning and relationships.

terms.name: Semantic Property
terms.description: property that defines a relationship or attribute with specific logical meaning in an ontology.

terms.name: Semantic Resource Identifier
terms.description: naming concept that provides a globally unique string for identifying a resource in semantic models.

terms.name: Semantic Web
terms.description: paradigm of a web of data that machines can understand and process.

terms.name: Serialization Format
terms.description: semantic modeling component representing a concrete syntax format for encoding and storing semantic data.

terms.name: Shape
terms.description: validation mechanism that defines a set of constraints for what valid data should look like for a particular use case.

terms.name: Standard
terms.description: semantic modeling component providing formal specification and recommendation that defines how semantic technologies should be implemented and used, developed by bodies like the W3C to ensure interoperability.

terms.name: SubClassOf
terms.description: model element relationship indicating that one class is a specialization or subset of another.

terms.name: Subject
terms.description: triple component that identifies the resource being described, typically a URI or blank node.

terms.name: Subject Heading
terms.description: knowledge organization system term or phrase used to describe the subject matter of resources in a catalog or database.

terms.name: Symmetric Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if A relates to B, then B relates to A

terms.name: T-Box
terms.description: knowledge representation component of a knowledge base that defines the vocabulary, classes, and properties.

terms.name: Taxonomy
terms.description: knowledge organization system that provides a hierarchical classification system organizing concepts into parent-child relationships.

terms.name: Thesaurus
terms.description: knowledge organization system organized by semantic relationships including synonyms, broader, and narrower terms.

terms.name: Transitive Property
terms.description: property characteristic where if A relates to B and B relates to C, then A relates to C.

terms.name: TriG
terms.description: serialization format that extends Turtle to support named graphs by grouping triples into graph blocks.

terms.name: Triple
terms.description: graph concept consisting of a subject, predicate, and object.

terms.name: Triplestore
terms.description: graph storage designed for storing and querying RDF triples efficiently.

terms.name: Turtle
terms.description: serialization format that provides a compact, human-readable text format for writing RDF.

terms.name: URI
terms.description: semantic resource identifier that provides a globally unique string for identifying a resource.

terms.name: Unnamed Individual
terms.description: individual represented by a blank node without a global URI identifier.

terms.name: Upper Ontology
terms.description: ontology that defines very general, domain-independent concepts like object, event, time, and space to provide a foundation for integration.

terms.name: Validation Mechanism
terms.description: semantic modeling process of checking whether data conforms to specified constraints, shapes, or rules.

terms.name: Value
terms.description: semantic modeling component representing the concrete data content assigned to properties, including literals and language-tagged strings.

terms.name: Value Set
terms.description: validation mechanism representing a defined collection of allowed values for a property.

terms.name: Vocabulary
terms.description: knowledge organization system that collects terms and their definitions used within a particular domain or application.

terms.name: broadMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is broader in meaning than another across different concept schemes.

terms.name: broader
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is more general than another within the same concept scheme.

terms.name: closeMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts are sufficiently similar to be used interchangeably in some applications.

terms.name: exactMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts have the same meaning and can be used interchangeably across different schemes.

terms.name: narrowMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is narrower in meaning than another across different concept schemes.

terms.name: narrower
terms.description: linking property indicating that one concept is more specific than another within the same concept scheme.

terms.name: related
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts are associated in meaning within the same concept scheme.

terms.name: relatedMatch
terms.description: linking property indicating that two concepts are related in meaning across different concept schemes.

terms.name: sameAs
terms.description: linking property indicating that two URIs refer to the same real-world entity.
